entry.title: An AI agent that rebooks passengers in ABAP, and waits for your approval first
entry.content:
A flight is cancelled and nine passengers have to be moved. There are only six free seats on the alternative flights, spread over three flights and three days. Someone has to decide who goes where, and someone has to make the change in the booking system.

That is a good task for an agent, as long as the agent isn't the one who presses the button. With the September 2026 release of CAP, the agent and the approval step can both be declared in CDS. I built a small demo, Flight Rescue, to see how far that gets you against a real ABAP system:

  • A CAP-level agent (@cap-js/agents) reads the affected bookings from an ABAP Platform Trial through a custom RAP service.
  • It proposes a rebooking plan and pauses for a dispatcher to approve (@ Agent.hitl).
  • Only after approval does CAP call a RAP action that moves each booking, one at a time.
  • A SAPUI5 cockpit shows the whole flow on one screen, including a seat map that fills up as ABAP confirms each move.

The cockpit with the agent's plan waiting for approval. Each dot on the right is a seat, read from ABAP; the orange ones are the nine affected passengers.

 

What's new in the September 2026 release, and what this demo uses


FeatureStatus in the releaseUsed here for
CAP-level agents (@cap-js/agents ) : @ Agent on a CDS service gives you a ReAct loop in your CAP server, served over A2AGamma (Node.js); Java is AlphaThe rebooking agent
@ Agent.hitl: human approval before an action runsNode.js onlyApprove or reject the plan
MCP adapter: the generic describe, query (now in CQL) and call toolsGenerally availableThe agent's tools, generated from the service
Chat preview for local developmentAlpha / experimentalTesting the agent before the cockpit existed

 

Everything else is plain CAP and RAP: a remote OData V4 service, an in-memory SQLite database for the plans, and a freestyle SAPUI5 page.

 

The architecture

The ABAP side is a custom RAP business object over a Z copy of /DMO/BOOKING. It has one action, rebook, which moves a booking to another flight. The action checks everything itself: the booking still exists and isn't cancelled, it is still on the expected flight, and the target flight exists, flies the same route and has a free seat. CAP never writes to ABAP in any other way.

 

1. An agent is a CDS service with one annotation

This is the whole agent definition, apart from the system prompt:

/**
 * You are the rebooking assistant for cancelled flights. ...
 * (the doc comment is the system prompt)
 */
@agent
@agent.connect: 'none'
@requires: 'Dispatcher'
service RebookAgentService {
  @readonly entity Disruptions as projection on fr.Disruptions excluding { plans };
  @readonly entity Plans       as projection on fr.Plans excluding { agentTask };
  @readonly entity PlanItems   as projection on fr.PlanItems;

  /** The disruption, its affected bookings and the only valid alternative flights. Changes nothing. */
  function disruptionImpact(disruption : UUID) returns fr.Impact;

  /** Save a Pending rebooking plan. Nothing changes in the booking system. */
  action proposeRebooking(disruption : UUID, assignments : many fr.Assignment, rationale : String) returns fr.ProposalResult;

  /** Request human approval to run this task's Pending plan in the booking system. */
  @AGent.hitl
  action applyRebooking(plan : UUID) returns fr.ApplyResult;
}

When the server starts, the plugin does three things:

  1. It builds tools from the service: the generic MCP tools describe and query for the entities, and one tool per function or action.
  2. It runs a ReAct loop with the configured LLM.
  3. It serves the agent over A2A at /a2a/rebook-agent, plus the chat preview in development.

The LLM comes from cds.requires.llm. In this demo it points at the Anthropic model implementation that ships with the plugin, with claude-opus-5-5, because I ran everything locally. On SAP BTP you'd use the documented kind: aicore instead, which goes through SAP AI Core and is the default in the production and hybrid profiles. In development, the default kind: auto picks up the credentials of a local Claude Code or OpenCode installation, so you may not need any configuration at all.

@requires: 'Dispatcher' works as it does on any CAP service: a user without the role can't talk to the agent at all.

What I like most here is that the agent can read only the three projections and call the three operations. It has no SQL connection, no generic HTTP client and no ABAP credentials. If something isn't in the service, the agent can't do it.

Two notes on the annotations:

  • @ Agent.connect: 'none' keeps the agent narrow: no extra MCP servers, no subagents. The plugin reads this annotation, but at the time of writing it isn't in the capire guide, so check that it still exists before you rely on it.
  • I included no AGENTS.md, on purpose. The release also lets you put an AGENTS.md and skills/*/SKILL.md files next to the service. When AGENTS.md is present, the plugin builds the agent from that directory instead of the generic ReAct agent. That is the right choice for a rich assistant like the XTravels sample. For a single, narrow job, the service's doc comment as the system prompt was enough.

 

2. The model sees CQL, not OData

The MCP adapter is generally available (GA) in this release, and its query tool now takes CQL. In the server log you can watch the agent work it out: it describes the entity, queries it, and then calls the custom functions:

[agents] - RebookAgentService request { method: 'message/send', text: 'LH 0402 on 2026-12-31 is cancelled. Rebook the passengers.' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService describe { entities: [ 'Disruptions' ] }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService query {
  cql: "SELECT ID, carrierId, connectionId, flightDate, airportFrom, airportTo, reason, status FROM Disruptions
        WHERE carrierId = 'LH' AND connectionId = '0402' AND flightDate = '2026-12-31'"
}
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call disruptionImpact { disruption: '4538ad9d-…' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call proposeRebooking { disruption: '4538ad9d-…', assignments: [ … ] }

This log is unedited apart from line breaks. I didn't write any tool code for describe or query.

 

What the ReAct loop is doing here

ReAct stands for "Reasoning and Acting": the model works in rounds. In each round it reads the conversation so far and either asks for a tool call or writes its final answer. The server runs the tool, adds the result to the conversation, and the next round starts. The model never executes anything itself. It only asks, and CAP decides.

The loop runs inside the CAP server. The plugin builds it with LangGraph and keeps the conversation and checkpoints in CAP's database. In every round the model gets the same three things:

  • the system prompt, which is the service's doc comment
  • the five tools generated from the service
  • the conversation so far, including every earlier tool result

The log above, round by round:

     
RoundThe model asks forWhat CAP does
1describe DisruptionsReturns the entity's fields
2query with a CQL SELECT … FROM Disruptions WHERE …Runs it on the service, with the dispatcher's authorisations
3disruptionImpactMy handler reads the bookings from ABAP and returns the 9 bookings and the only valid alternatives
4proposeRebookingMy handler checks the plan against the rules and saves it as Pending
5applyRebookingDoesn't run it. The loop stops here and waits for a human (next section)
6after ApproveRuns the action, which moves the bookings in ABAP
7the final answerShows the summary in the chat

 

The model decides the order of the calls, so two runs can take different paths and produce different plans. What it may call is fixed, though. There are only five tools, and each one goes through ordinary CAP handlers and @requires checks.

 

3. @ Agent.hitl: the pause

Here is the part that makes this usable for something that changes business data. Because applyRebooking is annotated @ Agent.hitl, the action doesn't run when the model decides to call it. Instead, the A2A task goes to the input-required state, and the pending call (including the plan ID) is in the task's status message:

task.status.state                                   // 'input-required'
task.status.message.metadata['sap.cds.agents.hitl']
    .actionRequests[0].args.plan                    // the plan waiting for approval

Any A2A client can then resume the same task with an approval or a rejection. In the cockpit, those are two JSON-RPC message/send calls:

approve: task => send([{ kind: 'text', text: 'approve' }], task),
reject: (task, message) => send([{ kind: 'data', data: { decisions: [{ type: 'reject', message }] } }], task)

send adds the task's taskId and contextId.

Prompts aren't a good control, but this is. The system prompt does tell the model not to ask for confirmation in text, but the guarantee doesn't depend on the model following it. Whatever the model writes, the action body doesn't run until a human resumes the task. With audit logging set up (I didn't in this demo), the plugin also records each approval or rejection as an AgentTaskResumed event.

I only had to put a UI on top. The cockpit shows the paused plan as a card with Approve and Reject, grouped by target flight, with the number of unassigned passengers and the agent's reasoning.

The paused task as the dispatcher sees it. The reasoning is the model's own; the numbers come from the server.

 

4. Approval

The domain rules are ordinary CAP code, and the agent can only choose among options the server has already checked:

  • disruptionImpact returns the affected bookings and the only valid alternatives: same route, same day up to two days later, seats left after other pending plans.
  • proposeRebooking refuses any booking, flight or seat count outside that list. It saves a Pending plan and changes nothing in ABAP.
  • The plan is bound to its agent task. The A2A task ID travels server-side, so it is never a tool argument. A resumed call that points at a different plan is refused (NOT_REVIEWED).
  • Each booking is moved with its expected current flight. If someone changed the booking in ABAP after the proposal, that one fails alone (STALE), and the rest still apply.
  • The model sees no customer data, only travel and booking IDs, flights and seat counts.

Because the agent is a CAP service, I could also tighten the generated tools with a normal CAP handler. The plugin raises a buildTools event, so a few lines check the tool list against an allowlist at startup and make the tool schemas strict, so unknown arguments are refused rather than dropped:

this.on('buildTools', async (req, next) => {
  const tools = await next()
  if (tools.map(t => t.name).join() !== TOOLS.join()) throw new Error('Agent tools differ from the allowlist')
  for (const t of tools) if (OPERATIONS.includes(t.name)) t.schema = t.schema.strict()
  return tools
})

 

5. Run against a real ABAP system

The agent's data access goes through one CAP remote service, ZFR_REBOOK. Its CDS model matches the $metadata of the published OData V4 binding.

  • Without credentials: cds watch mocks the service from the same contract. The mock applies the same checks and messages as the ABAP action, so the whole flow runs offline. The tests use a scripted model, so they need no API key either.
  • With credentials: set ABAP_URL, SAP_USER and SAP_PASSWORD as environment variables, and the same code talks to the ABAP Platform Trial.

In the run I recorded, the scenario was LH 0402 on FRA–EWR, with 9 bookings in three travels and 6 free seats on five alternatives. The agent proposed the following, and left 3 bookings unassigned with a reason:

  • travel 90000003 (2 bookings) → UA 0043, same day
  • travel 90000002 (3 bookings) → LH 0402, the next day
  • one booking of travel 90000001 → UA 0043, the next day

The plan isn't scripted. In the take shown in the GIF at the top, the agent split travel 90000001 across two flights and left travel 90000002 unassigned instead. Both plans stay within the seats the server listed, and that's the point: the model chooses, the server decides what it may choose from.

After Approve, the table in ABAP showed exactly those six moves, and the three alternatives were full. A Reject on a fresh scenario left all nine bookings where they were.

Before: the disruption is declared and nobody has moved yet.

After Approve: six orange seats have moved to the alternatives, which are now full, and three passengers are still on the cancelled flight. The agent's summary is in the chat.

 

Lessons learned

  • The A2A endpoint and browser logins. With mocked or basic authentication, the A2A endpoint answers 401 without a WWW-Authenticate challenge, so a browser never sends it the login it already uses for the OData service. A three-line middleware that adds the Basic challenge fixed it for local development. A deployed app with tokens doesn't need it.
  • RAP and leading zeros. The OData V4 binding returns NUMC fields without leading zeros ("TravelId":"4506") but accepts them with. I pad them in the one module that talks to ABAP.
  • Messages from RAP are cut at 50 characters when created with new_message_with_text, so keep the action's texts short. They end up in front of the dispatcher, and in front of the model.

 

A word on the SAP API Policy

The CAP documentation is explicit: CAP-level agents are meant for exposing custom CAP application services. They are not an SAP-endorsed pathway for agentic access to SAP Application APIs (section 2.2.2 of the SAP API Policy). This demo stays inside that line. The agent exposes only this app's own services, and the ABAP side is a custom Z RAP service over custom tables. For agentic access to SAP Application APIs, the CAP docs point to the reference architectures in the SAP Architecture Center.

 

Try it yourself

  • Code: https://github.com/Kamilkov/flight-rescue.git 
  • CAP release notes, September 2026: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/releases/2026/sep26
  • CAP-level agents guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-agents
  • MCP adapter guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-mcp

entry.title: Parallel Processing Technique and Its Application in a Business Process
entry.content:
Summary

This technical blog describes an approach to handling timeout issues that can occur during synchronous calls between BTP and SAP via an OData service.

Introduction

We may come across challenges when working on integration projects that involve synchronous operations. System A (in my example, the BTP environment) sends a request to System B (in my example, the SAP environment) and waits for a response.

The response waiting period becomes more challenging when the processing time required by System B is longer, which may be due to the amount of data being processed or the system load caused by other ongoing operations.

To overcome this, there are multiple approaches, such as reducing the amount of data to be processed, using asynchronous operations, or running the process during periods of lower system traffic.

However, the above approaches can sometimes be complex from a practical perspective, particularly when synchronous operation is required to process a large amount of data and maintain two-way communication between two different systems.

In my design, I have opted to address this issue using a "Parallel Processing" mechanism.

 

 

The above flow has been divided into two different systems (A & B). The parallel processing is covered in four different blocks in my current business scenario.

Execute RFC

  • This is an asynchronous Remote Function Module (RFC), developed using SE37 T-Code, which performs the task/posting defined in the source code section asynchronously.
  • Counter 1 is incremented for every call to this RFC. The data is processed and passed to the Call Back Function block.

Call Back Function

This is a simple Subroutine or Method within the calling program, which is responsible for capturing the Export Parameters/Tables content into a global table or variable. It acts as a container for the processed records.

Counter 2 is incremented within the Call Back Function routine to keep track of the processed data collected in the form of packets. This count is later compared with Counter 1 to ensure that the complete set of processed records has been received before exporting the data.

Below is the syntax that can be used to call the RFC along with the Call Back Function.

In my example, I have used the Call Back Function as a Method of the class.

              CALL FUNCTION 'Z_FM_RFC'
                STARTING NEW TASK 'ZTASK'
                DESTINATION IN GROUP DEFAULT
                CALLING zcl_class=>call_back
                ON END OF TASK
                EXPORTING
                  is_request                   = request                  
                TABLES
                  it_data                      = lt_data
                EXCEPTIONS
                  resource_failure             = 1
                  communication_failure        = 2
                  system_failure               = 3
                  OTHERS                       = 4.

              IF sy-subrc = 0.

                counter_1  = counter_1 + 1.

              ENDIF.

 

The following is a sample code demonstrating how the Call Back Function can be implemented and used.

  METHOD call_back.

    DATA:
      ls_process          TYPE BKPF,
      lt_returnmsg        TYPE bapiret2_tt.

    RECEIVE RESULTS FROM FUNCTION
        'ZFA_FM_RFC'
      IMPORTING
        es_process           = ls_process
      TABLES
        et_returnmsg         = lt_returnmsg.

*--------------------------------------------------------------------*
* Collect Messages
*--------------------------------------------------------------------*

    APPEND LINES OF lt_returnmsg
           TO mt_returnmsg.

*--------------------------------------------------------------------*
* Task Counter
*--------------------------------------------------------------------*

    counter_2 = counter_2 + 1.

  ENDMETHOD.

 

Further, until both counters, Counter 1 and Counter 2, become equal, a WAIT statement is used. Once both counters are equal, the complete set of processed records is passed back to System A.

Conclusion

With this approach, a combination of Asynchronous and Synchronous processing is achieved to process a large volume of data by sharing the processing load across the available work processes.

Below is the SAP documentation related to Parallel Processing.

https://help.sap.com/docs/ABAP_PLATFORM_NEW/7bfe8cdcfbb040dcb6702dada8c3e2f0/4d909309eba36e73e100000...

entry.title: Bringing abap2xlsx to ABAP Cloud (S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition): port, real-file tests and 30+ fixes
entry.content:
Why abap2xlsx on ABAP Cloud

abap2xlsx now runs on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition in ABAP Cloud (language version ABAP for Cloud Development), with 0 ATC findings and 197 green ABAP Unit tests. Every feature below was checked with real files opened in Microsoft Excel.

abap2xlsx is the de-facto open-source library (Apache-2.0) for creating and reading .xlsx files from ABAP, introduced on SAP Community in 2010 in abap2xlsx - Generate your professional Excel spreadsheet from ABAP. On-premise it is a given; on Public Cloud it cannot be imported as-is, because it uses classic iXML, codepage function modules, DDIC reads, WRITE statements and other APIs that are not released for ABAP Cloud.

This blog describes how I ported it (base version 7.16.0) into a customer package, how I tested it, and the 30+ bugs I found and fixed along the way. Most of those bugs also exist in the upstream code, so they are relevant for on-premise users too.

Porting: what had to be replaced

The port keeps the public API of abap2xlsx (ZCL_EXCEL, ZCL_EXCEL_WORKSHEET, writers and readers) and swaps every unreleased dependency for a released one.

Area Classic / on-premise ABAP Cloud replacement

XML DOMCL_IXML, IF_IXML_*CL_IXML_CORE, IF_IXML_*_CORE
XML parse of existing parts (XLSM)CL_XML_DOCUMENTiXML core parser
CodepagesCL_ABAP_CODEPAGE, CL_ABAP_CONV_IN_CE / OUT_CE, SCMS_*CL_ABAP_CONV_CODEPAGE
Field catalog, labelsDFIES, X031L, DDIF_*, SALVRTTI + XCO_CP_ABAP_DICTIONARY
Number / date outputWRITE ... TO, DESCRIBEstring templates, lines( )
MIME types of imagesSDOK_MIMETYPE_GETsmall internal map (png, jpg, gif, ...)
ALV bindingBIND_ALV, BIND_ALV_OLE2removed (no SALV/OLE in the cloud)
File accessLOAD_FILEraises an exception; use LOAD( xstring )
Font metrics for auto widthSAPscript metrics (TFO01)estimate from length and font size

A few DDIC details also needed care: data elements based on FLAG, TEXT80 or TEXT10 were switched to ABAP_BOOLEAN or built-in types, because the originals are not released.

One surprise: dynamic CREATE DATA ... TYPE HANDLE fails with CX_SY_CREATE_DATA_ERROR for unreleased types such as SYST_INDEX, which you hit simply by passing sy-index to set_cell. The port copies such values through CL_ABAP_ELEMDESCR=>GET_BY_KIND instead.

How I tested: real files, not only green syntax checks

A clean activation says little about an Excel library, so every feature was tested end to end with files a person opened in Excel.

  1. A test class ZCL_EXCEL_DEMO_CLOUD_TEST (IF_OO_ADT_CLASSRUN) builds one workbook per feature area and prints it as base64 in the ADT console.
  2. Each workbook is read back with ZCL_EXCEL_READER_2007 and written again (round trip), so reader and writer are tested against each other.
  3. The files are decoded locally and checked three ways: XML well-formedness per part, feature comparison with Python/openpyxl, and a final look in Excel (no "We found a problem" repair dialog).
  4. A file created by Excel itself (values, formulas, table, chart, comments, conditional formats, external link) is embedded in the class to test the reader on something abap2xlsx did not write.
  5. Every bug fix gets an ABAP Unit test in the same class; ATC runs with the variant ABAP_CLOUD_DEVELOPMENT_DEFAULT.

Feature areas covered: basic values and styles, CSV, charts, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, sheet and workbook protection, page setup and header/footer, comments, row and column outlines, autofilter, tables, rich text, merged cells, images (one-cell, two-cell and absolute anchor, header/footer images), freeze panes, column widths, named ranges, gradient fills and text rotation, XLSM with a VBA project, and 50,000-row files.

Tip: in the ATC run, choose the variant explicitly. In my system the default variant returned 0 findings although real findings existed.

Bugs found and fixed

The real-file tests found more than 30 defects; the ones below are in the upstream code as well, not caused by the port.

Area What went wrong Visible effect

ChartsEmpty invertIfNegative, smooth, symbol attributesExcel repairs the drawing
Data validationshowDropDown="1" written for list validationsDropdown arrow hidden
Conditional formattingEmpty cfvo val=""; reader ignored text rules (containsText ...)Repair dialog; rules lost on round trip
Protection / page setupReader did not read sheet/workbook protection, header/footer, printOptionsLost on round trip
OutlineoutlineLevelRow/Col never writtenOutline buttons missing
AutofilterText filters (Laptop* OR *Mouse) not written or readWrong rows hidden, no filter icon
TablesReader counted the totals row as data; nofilters and column formulas lostDuplicated totals row after round trip
Rich textShared-string numbers out of order when the same text had different formatsWrong formatting on another cell
Rich textget_cell did not clear et_rtf; partial fonts wrote sz="0", rFont=""Runs of the previous cell returned
Mergeset_merge( ip_formula = ... ) stored the formula as text; writers called delete_merge( ) while writingFormula shown as text; merges gone after a second write
ImagesAbsolute anchor written as a two-cell anchor without <to>; footer image used the left imageInvalid drawing; dump
Header/footerFooter and even pages built from the odd header string; font names lost their blanksFooter text lost, &G duplicated
Column widthAuto size never calculated; columns without width got 9.10; defaultColWidth not readAutosize columns 9.10 wide
XLSMWriter overrode create with an old copy that referenced a non-existing drawingCorrupt .xlsm package
Round trip of Excel filesExternal links, chart style/colour parts and chart XML dropped#REF!-risk, chart style reset
Huge-file writerFormulas written as attribute f="...", t="", dump with any header/footer, no autofilter/conditional formats/validations/commentsFormulas lost, missing features

Each fix is covered by an ABAP Unit test that checks the XML part or reads the file back.

Using it from RAP: an Excel download in a Fiori app

The easiest way to hand the file to a user is a custom entity with a largeObject field; Fiori elements then shows a download link per row.

@ObjectModel.query.implementedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_MY_EXCEL_QUERY'
define custom entity ZC_MY_EXCEL_REPORT
{
  key CompanyCode : bukrs;
  key Customer    : kunnr;
      @Semantics.largeObject: { mimeType: 'Mimetype', fileName: 'Filename',
                                contentDispositionPreference: #ATTACHMENT }
      Attachment  : abap.rawstring(0);
      @Semantics.mimeType: true
      Mimetype    : abap.char(128);
      Filename    : abap.char(128);
}
METHOD if_rap_query_provider~select.
  ...
  LOOP AT lt_result ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_row>).
    " always fill the MIME type - without it the stream link is not shown
    <ls_row>-mimetype = 'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet'.
    <ls_row>-filename = |Report_{ <ls_row>-companycode }.xlsx|.
    " build the file only when the client asks for the stream
    IF line_exists( lt_requested[ table_line = 'ATTACHMENT' ] ).
      <ls_row>-attachment = build_xlsx( <ls_row> ).   " ZCL_EXCEL + ZCL_EXCEL_WRITER_2007
    ENDIF.
  ENDLOOP.
  io_response->set_data( lt_result ).
ENDMETHOD.

Two things matter. First, fill Mimetype in every row: an empty MIME type hides the download link. Second, the media request reads a single entity by its keys only, so the query provider must handle a key-only filter and build the file just for that row.

Performance: 50,000 rows in about 7 seconds

After tuning, a 50,000-row x 10-column workbook is built in about 9 s and written in about 7 s with the huge-file writer.

 

 

Source: ZCL_EXCEL_DEMO_CLOUD_PERF, 20,000 set_cell calls per type, same system run.

The biggest cost was date and time cells: set_cell rebuilt the date number format style for every single cell, walking all styles with RTTI. A small cache per worksheet, one RTTI call per cell and typed local variables instead of CREATE DATA fixed that.

Step (50,000 rows x 10 columns) Before After

Build data with set_cell38 s9 s
Write with ZCL_EXCEL_WRITER_200718 s18 s
Write with ZCL_EXCEL_WRITER_HUGE_FILEnot usable7 s
Read with ZCL_EXCEL_READER_200733 s26 s
Read with ZCL_EXCEL_READER_HUGE_FILEnot measured12 s

Times vary by about 1.5x with system load. For large exports use ZCL_EXCEL_WRITER_HUGE_FILE: it writes the cells with a simple transformation and now takes all other sheet parts (autofilter, conditional formats, validations, comments, protection) from the 2007 writer, so the files match.

Lessons learned

  • Test with the target application, not only with the library. Most defects produced files that abap2xlsx itself read back fine, but that Excel repaired or displayed wrongly.
  • Round trips find reader bugs cheaply. Writing, reading and writing again, then comparing both outputs, exposed every attribute the reader silently dropped.
  • Activate classes with cyclic dependencies together. abap2xlsx classes reference each other; single-object activation can report success while objects stay inactive. A mass activation of all changed objects in one request avoids that.
  • Mind sy-tabix after method calls. One bug came from reading sy-tabix after cl_abap_zip->add( ), which had changed it; copy the index into a local variable first.
  • Arithmetic into a string target changes the calculation type. lv_string = lv_int * 609600 produced 4876800.0; wrap the expression in CONV int8( ) or a string template.
  • Simple transformations are strict about order. An attribute written after a child element raises CX_ST_INVALID_XML (OpenAttribute), and a relative path inside tt:ref raises CX_ST_REF_ACCESS.
  • The ADT classrun console escapes & as &. Measure string lengths before you "fix" an escaping bug that does not exist.

Limitations and next steps

The port is usable for productive exports today; a few gaps remain.

  • Auto column width is an estimate (characters x font size, +10% for bold), because SAPscript font metrics are not available in ABAP Cloud.
  • LOAD_FILE and ALV binding are not available; pass the file as xstring and bind internal tables with bind_table.
  • The 2007 reader and writer build a full iXML DOM, so they need roughly 20-30 s for 50,000 x 10 cells; use the huge-file writer and reader for large volumes.
  • Header/footer images on first pages (FIRST) are not read.

Next, I plan to offer the fixes that also apply on-premise back to the abap2xlsx repository as pull requests.

Have you run abap2xlsx on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition or on BTP ABAP Environment? I would like to hear which features you use and which problems you hit - please share them in the comments.
Github: https://github.com/cuongus/abap2xlsx_cloud

References

  • abap2xlsx on GitHub - source code of the library (Apache-2.0), base of this port; documentation at abap2xlsx.github.io
  • abap2xlsx - Generate your professional Excel spreadsheet from ABAP - original SAP Community blog by Ivan Femia, 12 July 2010

entry.title: Implementing Change Logs in RAP on SAP BTP ABAP Environment
entry.content:
I had a requirement in one of my RAP applications to display the change history of a business object.

The Change Log needed to show the field name, old value, new value, changed by, changed date/time, and the action performed.

I checked the available options and decided to use the Change Document Object instead of creating a separate custom table for maintaining the history.

In this post, I will share how I configured the Change Document Object in SAP BTP ABAP Environment, connected it with the RAP behavior definition, and displayed the change history using a RAP Custom Entity and Query Provider.

Create Change Document Object

I created the Change Document Object in ADT and added the required table and fields.

Add Change Documents in Behavior Definition

After creating the Change Document Object, I added it to the RAP behavior definition.

changedocuments master (ZCHANGE_LOG_OBJECT)

{

  changedocuments(

    create:key,

    update:data,

    delete:none

  );

}

create:key is used for creation, while update:data is used to capture the changed data. Delete logging was not required for this scenario.

Change Document Data Element

In ADT, open the relevant data element and enable the Change Document / Change Document Logging setting for the data element.

I missed this initially, and the field was not being recorded in the Change Document data even though the Change Document Object and behavior definition were configured.

After enabling change logging for the required data elements and regenerating the Change Document Object, the field changes were available in the Change Document data.

RAP Custom Entity

To display the Change Log in the application, I created a RAP Custom Entity.

@ObjectModel.query.implementedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_CHANGE_LOG_QUERY'

define custom entity ZI_CHANGE_LOG

{
  key ChangeDocNumber : abap.char(10);
  key ChangeDocItem   : abap.char(70);
  key FieldName       : abap.char(50);
      @UI.hidden: true
      BusinessObjectId : abap.char(90);
      @UI.hidden: true
      ChangedDate : abap.dats;
      @UI.hidden: true
      ChangedTime : abap.tims;
      ChangedOn : abap.char(20);
      ChangedBy : abap.char(12);
      OldValue  : abap.string;
`
      NewValue  : abap.string;

      Action    : abap.char(20);

}

Query Provider

The query provider implements:

ABAP CLASS

INTERFACES if_rap_query_provider.

The main logic is inside:

abap

METHOD if_rap_query_provider~select.
DATA(lo_filter) = io_request->get_filter( ).
IF lo_filter IS BOUND.
  DATA(lt_ranges) = lo_filter->get_as_ranges( ).
  LOOP AT lt_ranges INTO DATA(ls_name_range).
    CASE ls_name_range-name.
      WHEN 'BUSINESSOBJECTID'.
        LOOP AT ls_name_range-range
          INTO DATA(ls_object_range).
          IF ls_object_range-sign = 'I'
             AND ls_object_range-option = 'EQ'.
            lv_object_id = ls_object_range-low.
          ENDIF.
        ENDLOOP.
    ENDCASE.
  ENDLOOP.
ENDIF.
I use the business object ID so that the query only reads the change history belonging to the current object.

Reading Change Documents

cl_chdo_read_tools=>changedocument_read(
  EXPORTING
    i_objectclass   = 'ZCHANGE_LOG_OBJECT'

    it_objectid     = lt_objid

  IMPORTING

    et_cdredadd_tab = lt_redadd

  CHANGING

    ct_cdhdr        = lt_cdhdr

).
The header and item data are then mapped to the Custom Entity.
ls_result-ChangedDate = ls_hdr-udate.

ls_result-ChangedTime = ls_hdr-utime.

ls_result-ChangedBy   = ls_hdr-username.

ls_result-ChangeDocNumber = ls_item-changenr.

ls_result-ChangeDocItem   = ls_item-tabkey.

ls_result-FieldName       = ls_item-fname.

ls_result-OldValue = ls_item-value_shstr_old.

ls_result-NewValue = ls_item-value_shstr_new.

CASE ls_item-chngind.
  WHEN 'I'.
    ls_result-Action = 'Created'.
  WHEN 'U'.
    ls_result-Action = 'Changed'.

  WHEN 'D'.
    ls_result-Action = 'Deleted'.
ENDCASE.  

 

Sorting and Paging

I also handled sorting so that the latest changes are displayed first.

SORT lt_result BY

  ChangedDate     DESCENDING

  ChangedTime     DESCENDING

  ChangeDocNumber DESCENDING

  ChangeDocItem   DESCENDING.

Paging is handled using the RAP request paging information.

Result

Finally, the Change Log is displayed in the Fiori application.

The result shows the field, old value, new value, action, user and date/time.

Conclusion

That's how I implemented the Change Log for my RAP application in the SAP BTP ABAP Environment.

The Change Document Object handles the change information, and I used CL_CHDO_READ_TOOLS to read it and expose it through the RAP Custom Entity.

Hope this helps if you are working on a similar requirement.

entry.title: GeoTrack: tracking trips in SAP HANA Cloud
entry.content:
GeoTrack is a portfolio project with exactly one user: me.

  • My iPhone records where I go.
  • My Apple Watch records my walks and hikes, and I pick the photos I want to keep.
  • Everything lands in SAP HANA Cloud.
  • Its spatial engine, which lets SQL store and measure points, lines and areas, turns raw positions into zones, trips and routes.
  • A RAP business object on an ABAP system records my visits to selected places.
  • A Fiori Elements app shows each trip with its route on a map, my heart rate, the altitude profile, the photos and the weather of every hour.
  • Claude, Anthropic's AI model, can answer questions about my trips through MCP tools.

I did not write GeoTrack's code. I decided what it should do and approved each design, and Claude wrote the code and the tests in Claude Code, from the HANA model and the RAP object to the Fiori app and the iOS app. I ran it on my own server and phone and checked the results.

This post walks through both versions of the architecture, explains why I asked Claude to replace two off-the-shelf senders with one iOS app, and shows the HANA spatial SQL that does the actual work.

The coordinates in the SQL examples are made up. The screenshots show real trips.

 

What GeoTrack does

  • Positions. Every position from the phone is stored as an ST_POINT in HANA Cloud, also while the trial database sleeps at night.
  • Zones. Places such as home, the supermarket or a trailhead are circles or polygons. A position inside a private zone is coarsened to the zone's centre before it is written.
  • Trips. Positions are cut into walks and drives using the iOS motion activity, and each route is stored as a LINESTRING.
  • Visits. A confirmed stay in a selected zone becomes a SiteVisit, a RAP business object on an ABAP Platform trial system.
  • Weather. Every closed trip gets the hourly weather from Open-Meteo.
  • Workouts and photos. Apple Watch workouts (always hikes - I live in the mountains), with heart rate and GPS route, and my photos are linked to the trips they belong to.
  • Apps. A read-only Fiori Elements List Report and Object Page shows all of it, and MCP tools let Claude answer questions about it.

 

Version 1: three senders

The first version used the best existing app for each job.

Positions came from OwnTracks. In Move mode it publishes a position when I have moved 50 m or when 300 seconds have passed. It sent JSON over MQTT to a Mosquitto broker on my VPS. The CAP service subscribed and acknowledged a message only after HANA had committed it.

Workouts came from Health Auto Export. Its REST automation posted my Apple Watch workouts, with heart rate samples and the GPS route, to an endpoint of the CAP service. It synced about once an hour after I unlocked the phone.

Photos came through my Mac. I AirDropped the photos of a walk to the Mac and dragged them into an inbox folder. A launchd agent read their metadata, made a small thumbnail without metadata and posted it.

The MQTT path had one property I liked a lot. The HANA Cloud trial stops every night. While it slept, the broker kept the phone's messages, and the CAP service received them again once HANA was back. Nothing was lost, only delayed.

 

Why I asked Claude to build my own iOS app

Version 1 worked. It also had three setups, three ways to fail and a Mac in the loop. These are the reasons I decided to replace it.

  • One app instead of three channels. Version 1 meant a broker to run and secure, a paid app's automation, and photos that arrived only when my Mac was awake and I remembered to drag them. Now one app talks HTTPS to one server.
  • More evidence on every position. The server decides which positions to trust, so it needs evidence. The app sends more data: the fields OwnTracks sent, plus the speed accuracy, the course accuracy and how confident iOS is about the motion activity. The difference showed early in the side-by-side run. During a 15-minute stop at a shop, OwnTracks delivered four positions inside the shop's zone, none of them classified as walking, so the server could not confirm the visit. The app delivered fourteen, with walking detected within two minutes of arrival.
  • Control over the recorder. The app has three modes: Auto, Manual (it records, but sends only when I tap) and Paused. A status screen shows what is waiting and why an upload stopped.
  • No junk at night. One night the database recorded a one-kilometre drive while I was asleep. An offline phone indoors had reported positions at motorway speed. The server now ignores positions outside zones based on vertical accuracy. The app also goes to sleep at home. When the phone has had no network for a minute (airplane mode, my habit at night) and its last fix lay inside the home zone, the app switches location updates off. iOS region monitoring wakes it if I leave the zone, and the network wakes it in the morning. A position that is never recorded needs no filter, and a GPS that is off uses no battery.
  • No subscription. Health Auto Export's REST automation belongs to its paid tier. My own app needs only the Apple Developer membership I already have.

The status screen, from the iOS Simulator with synthetic data. Left: everything is sent. Right: the server rejects the token, so seven positions wait on the phone.

How the app is built

A thin recorder. The phone records, queues and uploads. Zones, privacy rules and trips stay on the server, where they can be rebuilt from the raw data at any time. The phone drops only what iOS itself marks as invalid. It keeps the rhythm OwnTracks had, one position every 50 m or 300 seconds.

The contracts of the apps it replaced. Positions go to a new POST /positions route in OwnTracks' JSON shape. Workouts use Health Auto Export's JSON shape, and photos the shape the Mac agent used. The server's zone lookup, coarsening and trip rules did not change.

A queue on the phone instead of a broker. Every kept position is first written to the phone as a small file. Batches of up to 50 go to the server, and a batch leaves the phone only when the server's answer accounts for every position in it. While HANA sleeps, the server answers 503 and the app tries again a minute later. The server stores a position once per device and timestamp, so a resend does no harm.

Apple's frameworks only. Claude wrote the app with SwiftUI, Core Location, Core Motion, HealthKit and the iOS photo picker, without third-party packages. The logic (the keep rule, the queues, the uploaders, the workout sync and the photo metadata) lives in a Swift package with 202 tests that run on the Mac. Photos are picked in the app, so it never needs access to the whole library. It sends an 800 px thumbnail with all metadata removed, and the original never leaves the phone.

The app is currently waiting for review in the iOS App Store and hopefully will be approved soon.

 

Architecture today

From the phone to the server. The app posts to three routes, /positions, /health/workouts and /photos, through Caddy with TLS and a bearer token. Each answer to /positions also names the home zone as a circle, which is how the app knows where it may sleep. The first position after a sleep carries OwnTracks' region trigger, and the server starts the next trip there, from home, instead of treating the quiet night as a gap in the data.

CAP on a VPS, HANA Cloud on SAP BTP. The application layer is one CAP service (Node.js) in a Docker container on a small Linux VPS, next to Caddy and an ABAP Platform trial system. Only the database lives on SAP BTP, as an HDI container on a HANA Cloud trial instance. The VPS already ran Docker, Caddy and the ABAP trial, so one more container there was simpler than a second platform. The price is real: no XSUAA, no Destination service, no App Router. For a project with one user that trade is fine. With a second user, XSUAA would come first.

Inside the CAP service.

  • The ingest parses each position, asks HANA for its zone, coarsens it inside a private zone and inserts it.
  • The segmenter is a pure function that walks a device's positions in time order and produces zone events and trips. It uses the motion activity, rules for stops and silences, and accuracy limits that differ inside and outside zones. A runner calls it ten seconds after new data arrives and sweeps every five minutes.
  • Each closed trip gets hourly weather from Open-Meteo, with the coordinates rounded to about 1 km.
  • A confirmed stay in a flagged zone goes into CAP's persistent outbox, which delivers it to the ABAP system.

RAP on ABAP Platform. SiteVisit is a managed RAP business object with a bound close action and ABAP Unit tests for its validations, published as an OData V4 Web API. CAP consumes it as a remote service. The visit's key is a UUID v5 derived from the zone event, so a repeated create or close does no harm, and the outbox keeps retrying for about 14 hours while the ABAP system is down.

Fiori Elements. The trips app is a read-only List Report and Object Page on a CAP OData V4 service, built with SAPUI5 1.152 and driven mostly by annotations. Custom sections add the route map (a sap.ui.vbm GeoMap with OpenStreetMap tiles), the heart rate and altitude/speed charts (sap.viz, with the value of each point on hover) and the photos. Caddy publishes the app behind a password.

The screenshots show real trips: a drive with its route (at the top of the article), and a hike recorded by the Apple Watch, with its heart rate, altitude and photos.

 

 

The stop at the end of the drive became a SiteVisit on the ABAP system. My walk inside the shop confirmed the stay, CAP created the visit, and the bound close action recorded the departure when I drove off nine minutes later. This is the record as the OData V4 Web API returns it (trimmed, times in UTC):

{
  "VisitUUID": "c401443f-6e02-5a7e-87e8-9084f477e218",
  "ZoneName": "Supermarket",
  "Device": "iphone",
  "ArrivedAt": "2026-09-23T17:08:37Z",
  "DepartedAt": "2026-09-23T17:17:51Z",
  "Duration": 9.233,
  "DurationUnit": "MIN",
  "Status": "C",
  "ExtEventKey": "iphone|1408ffba-…|enter|2026-09-23T17:08:37.000Z"
}

 

MCP tools. A curated, read-only CAP service, exposed through @cap-js/mcp, lets Claude on my Mac answer questions like "How far did I walk this month, compared with last month?" or "Was it raining on any of my walks?". The tools (totals, zoneStats, tripsNear, tripDetail and a generic query) return times, lengths and distances, never coordinates.

 

HANA spatial, with examples

What HANA spatial is

SAP HANA has a spatial engine built in. Besides numbers, text and dates, a column can hold a geometry: a point, a line or an area. SQL can then answer geometric questions, such as how far apart two points are, whether a point lies inside an area, or which routes passed near a place. In SAP HANA Cloud it is part of the database, including the free trial, so there is nothing to install and no separate GIS server to run.

Four ideas are enough to read the examples below.

  • Geometry types. ST_POINT holds a single point. ST_GEOMETRY holds any shape, for example a POLYGON for an area or a LINESTRING for a route.
  • A spatial reference system. Every geometry carries an SRID, a number that says what its coordinates mean. GeoTrack uses SRID 4326, which is WGS 84, the latitude and longitude that GPS delivers. HANA treats 4326 as a round-earth system: distances follow the curve of the earth and can come back in metres rather than degrees.
  • Well-known text (WKT). A readable notation for shapes, such as POINT (1.5034 42.5021). ST_GeomFromText turns WKT into a geometry, and ST_AsText turns a geometry back into WKT. The x coordinate comes first, so the longitude comes before the latitude.
  • ST_ functions. Their names follow the SQL/MM and OGC Simple Features standards, so most of them match PostGIS. HANA calls most of them as methods of a geometry: where PostGIS writes ST_Distance(a, b), HANA writes a.ST_Distance(b). A new point is written NEW ST_POINT(1.5034, 42.5021, 4326).

You can try all four in any HANA Cloud SQL console, without creating a table. This query makes up a park, a home inside it and a shop outside it:

WITH PLACES AS (
  SELECT ST_GeomFromText(
           'POLYGON((1.50 42.50, 1.51 42.50, 1.51 42.51, 1.50 42.51, 1.50 42.50))',
           4326) AS PARK,
         NEW ST_POINT(1.5034, 42.5021, 4326) AS HOME,
         NEW ST_POINT(1.5130, 42.5064, 4326) AS SHOP
    FROM DUMMY)
SELECT ROUND(HOME.ST_Distance(SHOP, 'meter')) AS METRES,
       PARK.ST_Intersects(HOME) AS HOME_IN_PARK,
       PARK.ST_Intersects(SHOP) AS SHOP_IN_PARK,
       HOME.ST_AsText() AS HOME_WKT
  FROM PLACES;
-- METRES  HOME_IN_PARK  SHOP_IN_PARK  HOME_WKT
-- 922     1             0             POINT (1.5034 42.5021)

The home is 922 m from the shop, ST_Intersects answers 1 for the home and 0 for the shop, and the WKT puts the longitude first. In SRID 1000004326, SAP's planar version of WGS 84, the same HOME.ST_Distance(SHOP) returns 0.0105, in degrees.

GeoTrack needs only a handful of these functions: ST_Intersects to find a position's zone, ST_Distance for lengths and nearness, and WKT in both directions. HANA offers much more, from GeoJSON output to spatial clustering.

Doing this in the database keeps the work next to the data. Positions, zones and trips sit in ordinary tables, so one SQL statement can join them, filter by time and measure distances, instead of loading thousands of rows into application code.

In CAP, spatial columns use the types hana.ST_POINT and hana.ST_GEOMETRY. CAP does not write spatial values for you, so every spatial write in GeoTrack is native SQL through cds.db.run. Six patterns cover the whole project.

1. A point for every position

entity Positions {
  key device : String(40);
  key ts     : Timestamp;
      lat    : Decimal(9,6) not null;
      lon    : Decimal(9,6) not null;
  /** Position as ST_POINT, SRID 4326; set via native SQL on insert */
      point  : hana.ST_POINT(4326);
      // accuracy, altitude, speed, motion activity, zone, raw JSON, ...
}
INSERT INTO GEOTRACK_POSITIONS (DEVICE, TS, LAT, LON, POINT /* , ... */)
VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326) /* , ... */);
-- the point's parameters are (1.5034, 42.5021): longitude first

The first gotcha of the project: ST_POINT(x, y) takes the longitude first. The table keeps latitude and longitude as plain decimals as well, so the OData services and the Fiori app never touch the geometry type. In the SQL console the points read like this:

SELECT DEVICE, TS, POINT.ST_AsText() AS WKT
  FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS
 ORDER BY TS DESC;
-- POINT (1.5034 42.5021)

2. Which zone is this position in?

A zone is a circle or a polygon, and both live in one geometry column. For a circle, the service computes a 32-point polygon from the centre and the radius, and HANA parses the WKT. Here is a 200 m circle:

UPDATE GEOTRACK_ZONES SET GEOM = ST_GeomFromText(?, 4326) WHERE ID = ?;
-- 'POLYGON((1.5034 42.5039, 1.5038 42.5039, 1.5042 42.5038, ..., 1.5034 42.5039))'

Every incoming position asks HANA for its zone before it is inserted:

SELECT TOP 1 ID, ISPRIVATE, ISBASE, CENTRELAT, CENTRELON
  FROM GEOTRACK_ZONES
 WHERE GEOM IS NOT NULL
   AND GEOM.ST_Intersects(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326)) = 1
 ORDER BY ISPRIVATE DESC,
          CASE WHEN KIND = 'polygon' THEN 0 ELSE RADIUSM END ASC;

Zones overlap, so the ORDER BY decides. A private zone beats a public one, a polygon beats any circle, and among circles the smallest wins. When the winner is private, the position is written with the zone's centre instead of its own coordinates, and its raw JSON loses the coordinates and the Wi-Fi network's name and address. The real values are never stored.

3. A trip's length and line in one statement

When the segmenter closes a trip that only the phone recorded, HANA measures it (simplified): 

SELECT
  (SELECT ROUND(SUM(D)) FROM (
      SELECT POINT.ST_Distance(LAG(POINT) OVER (ORDER BY TS), 'meter') AS D
        FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS WHERE TRIP_ID = ?)) AS LENGTH_M,
  (SELECT 'LINESTRING(' || STRING_AGG(LON || ' ' || LAT, ', ' ORDER BY TS) || ')'
     FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS WHERE TRIP_ID = ?) AS ROUTE_WKT
FROM DUMMY;

UPDATE GEOTRACK_TRIPS SET ROUTE = ST_GeomFromText(ROUTEWKT, 4326) WHERE ID = ?;

 ST_Distance with LAG over the time order measures every step in metres, and the outer SUM adds up the path in one pass. STRING_AGG ... ORDER BY builds the WKT that becomes the LINESTRING and also the line the Fiori map draws. When the Apple Watch recorded a route during the trip, its denser points take over from the phone's for that stretch. That stitching runs in JavaScript, and every trip records whether its length came from the phone, the Watch or both.

4. Which trips passed near a place?

This query sits behind the MCP tool tripsNear. For every trip in a date range, it finds the position closest to a given point and keeps the trips that came within the radius (trimmed):

SELECT ID, STARTEDAT, KIND, LENGTHM, TS, D FROM (
  SELECT T.ID, T.STARTEDAT, T.KIND, T.LENGTHM, P.TS,
         P.POINT.ST_Distance(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326), 'meter') AS D,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY T.ID
           ORDER BY P.POINT.ST_Distance(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326), 'meter'), P.TS) AS RN
    FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P
    JOIN GEOTRACK_TRIPS T ON T.ID = P.TRIP_ID
   WHERE T.ENDEDAT IS NOT NULL AND T.STARTEDAT >= ? AND T.STARTEDAT < ?)
 WHERE RN = 1 AND D <= ?
 ORDER BY D;

 A point goes in, and distances and times come out. When I ask about a place by name, Claude supplies its coordinates, calls the tool and answers with times and distances, without seeing a single one of my positions.

5. A set-based backfill instead of a correlated TOP 1

Zones came after the first positions, so every stored position needed its best zone. Claude's first attempt was a correlated subquery with TOP 1 ... ORDER BY, which HANA rejects. A MERGE over a ROW_NUMBER ranking does the same job in one statement, with the same precedence as the live lookup:

MERGE INTO GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P USING (
  SELECT DEVICE, TS, ID FROM (
    SELECT P.DEVICE, P.TS, Z.ID,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY P.DEVICE, P.TS
             ORDER BY Z.ISPRIVATE DESC,
                      CASE WHEN Z.KIND = 'polygon' THEN 0 ELSE Z.RADIUSM END) AS RN
      FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P
      JOIN GEOTRACK_ZONES Z
        ON Z.GEOM IS NOT NULL AND P.POINT.ST_Intersects(Z.GEOM) = 1
     WHERE P.ZONE_ID IS NULL)
   WHERE RN = 1) S
ON P.DEVICE = S.DEVICE AND P.TS = S.TS
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ZONE_ID = S.ID;

6. Thousands of points in one round trip

Positions are stored one per database round trip, about five per second when Claude measured it, which is plenty for batches of 50. A two-hour workout from the Watch can bring more than 7,000 route points. The workout route therefore inserts its rows without geometry and builds every point in one statement:

UPDATE GEOTRACK_WORKOUTROUTE
   SET POINT = NEW ST_POINT(TO_DOUBLE(LON), TO_DOUBLE(LAT), 4326)
 WHERE WORKOUT_ID = ?;

A workout of that size is stored in about five seconds. The private-zone check for its points runs in JavaScript against the zone polygons, which the service reads once per workout with GEOM.ST_AsWKT(), instead of making 7,000 ST_Intersects round trips.

HANA lessons in one list

  • ST_POINT(x, y) is (longitude, latitude).
  • No TOP or ORDER BY in a correlated subquery. Rank with ROW_NUMBER() and apply with MERGE.
  • In native SQL, BOOLEAN columns want the literals TRUE and FALSE, not 1 and 0.
  • AT is a reserved word, so a column named at must be quoted everywhere.
  • Timestamps come back without an offset. Parse them as UTC explicitly instead of letting JavaScript guess.
  • A trial instance stops every night. Design every writer for it.

 

Privacy by design

This is real personal data, so privacy lives in the write path.

  • Coarsening happens before the insert. Real coordinates inside a private zone are never written, and neither are the Wi-Fi network's name and hardware address (a BSSID can be geolocated through public databases).
  • Watch route points inside a private zone are coarsened the same way, and a photo taken inside one is not stored at all.
  • Photos travel as 800 px thumbnails without metadata, stripped on the phone and again on the server.
  • Open-Meteo receives one coordinate per trip hour, rounded to about 1 km.
  • The MCP tools never return coordinates.
  • The repository contains no real data. The tests use synthetic coordinates.

 

What I would tell someone starting a similar project

  • Keep the rules on the server. When the senders changed, HANA and the segmenter stayed as they were.
  • Copy the contract of the tool you replace. Then run old and new side by side under different device names and compare.
  • Let HANA do the geometry, set-based. One statement over many rows beats a round trip per row.
  • Design for the database being away. A queue on the phone, idempotent writes and retries that span a night turn the nightly stop into a non-event.
  • Expect surprises in photo metadata. iOS's ImageIO does not expose the time-zone offset of a ProRAW photo. The app reads the EXIF data itself, and for an edited ProRAW photo it derives the offset from the photo's GPS time.

 

By the numbers

  • First commit on 22 September 2026. The app took over from the three senders on 6 October 2026.
  • 282 commits, 279 of them co-authored by Claude.
  • 12 tables and 29 views in one HDI container on a shared HANA Cloud trial instance: the data model's 11 entities and 6 views, a table for CAP's persistent queue, and a view for each of the 23 entities the services expose.

  • 347 JavaScript tests and 202 Swift tests. None of them needs HANA.
  • 1 RAP business object with a bound action, 1 Fiori Elements app and 1 iOS app with two screens.
  • 1 CAP service with 3 upload routes, OData V4 services for the Fiori app and the MCP tools, and an OData client for the ABAP system.

If you work with HANA Cloud spatial, run CAP outside Cloud Foundry, or build with Claude Code, I'd be glad to compare notes in the comments.

The free public repo (MIT license) 👉 https://github.com/Kamilkov/geotrack-location

entry.title: Goodbye BAPI_PO_CREATE1? Four things I learned creating purchase orders with MODIFY ENTITIES
entry.content:
Introduction

For most of my 16 years with ABAP, creating a purchase order from code meant one thing: BAPI_PO_CREATE1. It was always there, and it always worked.

But systems age. I like to think about legacy code the way physics thinks about entropy: left alone, everything drifts toward disorder, and keeping a system clean is a constant fight. Clean Core is SAP's name for that fight.

So when I checked the release contract of BAPI_PO_CREATE1 in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, I saw that entropy in a single line: since 2022-01-31 it is flagged C1 NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED, and the contract itself names the successor, I_PurchaseOrderTP_2.

I_PurchaseOrderTP_2 is a RAP business object released for ABAP Cloud (C1) since 2021-05-30, with 13 entities. So I tried it the way SAP wants: one MODIFY ENTITIES call, no BAPI. Most posts I find about EML use a custom BO. Here I used SAP's own, and that is where the surprises were. Everything below comes from real runs in my lab.

The setup: header and item in one call

System: S/4HANA 2023, SAP_BASIS 758. Document type NB, one item. I create the header and the item together: the header gets a content ID (%cid), and the item points to it with %cid_ref.

MODIFY ENTITIES OF i_purchaseordertp_2
  ENTITY purchaseorder
    CREATE FIELDS ( purchaseordertype companycode purchasingorganization
                    purchasinggroup supplier documentcurrency )
    WITH VALUE #( ( %cid                   = 'PO_1'
                    purchaseordertype      = 'NB'
                    companycode            = 'BRLF'
                    purchasingorganization = 'BRLF'
                    purchasinggroup        = 'BRG'
                    supplier               = '0000014000'
                    documentcurrency       = 'BRL' ) )
    CREATE BY \_purchaseorderitem
    FIELDS ( material plant orderquantity purchaseorderquantityunit
             netpriceamount taxcode )
    WITH VALUE #( ( %cid_ref = 'PO_1'
                    %target  = VALUE #( ( %cid                      = 'ITEM_1'
                                          material                  = iv_material
                                          plant                     = 'BAT1'
                                          orderquantity             = 1
                                          purchaseorderquantityunit = 'ST'
                                          netpriceamount            = '10.00'
                                          taxcode                   = 'I1' ) ) ) )
  MAPPED es_mapped
  FAILED es_failed
  REPORTED es_reported.

That is the whole create. The interesting part is everything around it.

Surprise 1: without COMMIT ENTITIES, nothing exists

The MODIFY returns no error, and MAPPED is filled. It looks done. It is not.

  • EKKO had 1,779 rows before the call and 1,779 after.
  • The PurchaseOrder field in MAPPED is empty. The only key you get is %pid, a preliminary ID.

Outside a RAP context (a report, a class, a job), you own the transaction. MODIFY only changes the transactional buffer; COMMIT ENTITIES is what triggers the save. Forget it and you get no dump, no message, and no document.

Surprise 2: getting the PO number takes CONVERT KEY, and the item is different

I_PurchaseOrderTP_2 uses late numbering: the real number is only drawn during the save. To read it, you need the long form of COMMIT ENTITIES and CONVERT KEY between BEGIN and END.

For the header, %pid is enough:

COMMIT ENTITIES BEGIN
  RESPONSE OF i_purchaseordertp_2
    FAILED   DATA(ls_failed_late)
    REPORTED DATA(ls_reported_late).

LOOP AT ls_mapped-purchaseorder ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_m>).
  CONVERT KEY OF i_purchaseordertp_2 FROM <ls_m>-%pid TO DATA(ls_po_key).
  " ls_po_key-purchaseorder now holds the real number (45000016xx)
ENDLOOP.

For the item, I expected the same pattern to work. It dumped: CX_RAP_INVALID_PRELIMINARY_KEY, CONVERT_KEY_NOT_MAPPED. The item needs the temporary key, %pid plus the preliminary key from MAPPED:

LOOP AT ls_mapped-purchaseorderitem ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_mi>).
  CONVERT KEY OF i_purchaseorderitemtp_2
    FROM TEMPORARY VALUE #( %pid = <ls_mi>-%pid
                            %tmp = <ls_mi>-%key )
    TO DATA(ls_item_key).
ENDLOOP.
COMMIT ENTITIES END.

A tip from my own mistakes: run the item conversion last when you test it. A wrong CONVERT KEY dumps, and the ADT console loses everything it printed before.

One more thing: a dump in CONVERT KEY does not undo the purchase order. In my first run the item conversion dumped, and 4500001696 was still saved in EKKO. The save had already happened at COMMIT ENTITIES BEGIN. With FROM TEMPORARY, the item came back as 4500001698/00010.

Surprise 3: errors come early, and finding the failed instance is tricky

With a material that does not exist, the error arrives in the MODIFY itself, before any save. FAILED and REPORTED are filled, with these messages:

  • Header, MEPO/000: Purchase order still contains faulty items
  • Item, ME/062: Account assignment mandatory for material ZAAP_NAO_EXISTE (enter acc. ass. cat.)
  • Item, M3/305: The material ZAAP_NAO_EXISTE does not exist or is not activated

FAILED had three lines: one for the header and two for the same item, all with %fail-cause = UNSPECIFIC.

The catch: in FAILED, %cid comes back empty and %pid is zeroed. The only thing that told me which instance failed was the preliminary item key, Item = '00010'. If you create several items in one call, map errors back through that key, not through your %cid.

The errors are structured per entity and field (%element-material is flagged), and your code decides what to do. Nothing is written, and ROLLBACK ENTITIES cleans the buffer.

Surprise 4: you cannot commit from inside a behavior

A common idea is to call a released SAP BO from your own RAP BO, for example from an action, and commit right there. I tested both ways.

  • Directly in the handler, it does not even compile: The command "COMMIT-ENTITIES" is not allowed in a BEHAVIOR class.
  • Hidden in a normal class called by the handler, the compiler cannot see it. At runtime it dumps: BEHAVIOR_ILLEGAL_STATEMENT, Statement "COMMIT ENTITIES" is not allowed with this status, with the reason This contract violation always causes an error to occur.

Inside RAP, the framework owns the transaction. Your handler runs in the interaction phase, and the save happens later, once, for everything. If your BO needs to create a PO, do the MODIFY ENTITIES in the handler and let the framework commit.

Two small things worth knowing

No gaps in numbering. Across my test runs, four creations were undone with ROLLBACK ENTITIES. The three saved orders still got consecutive numbers: 4500001696, 4500001697 and 4500001698. With late numbering, a number is only drawn when the save really happens.

RESPONSE types in method signatures. On SAP_BASIS 758, writing TYPE RESPONSE FOR MAPPED EARLY directly in a METHODS signature does not compile (Unable to interpret "MAPPED"). Declaring a TYPES first works:

TYPES ty_mapped TYPE RESPONSE FOR MAPPED EARLY i_purchaseordertp_2.
TYPES ty_failed TYPE RESPONSE FOR FAILED EARLY i_purchaseordertp_2.

METHODS create_po
  IMPORTING iv_material TYPE matnr
  EXPORTING es_mapped   TYPE ty_mapped
            es_failed   TYPE ty_failed.

EML vs. BAPI, and conclusion

Point MODIFY ENTITIES on I_PurchaseOrderTP_2 BAPI_PO_CREATE1

Release statusC1 released since 2021-05-30C1 NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED since 2022-01-31, successor I_PURCHASEORDERTP_2
Usable in ABAP CloudYesNo
CommitCOMMIT ENTITIES / ROLLBACK ENTITIESBAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT / ROLLBACK

The create itself was one statement. What took my time was the transaction model: commit or nothing, late numbering, temporary keys and who owns the save. Once that is clear, EML on SAP's released BOs is a cleaner and future-proof way to create purchase orders, and of the two it is the only one you can use in ABAP Cloud.

For me, this is what Clean Core looks like in practice. Not a big migration, but one familiar call at a time, replaced by something SAP will keep alive. A small step against entropy.

Have you replaced a BAPI with a released RAP BO yet? Which one surprised you?

entry.title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud – A Strategic Overview (Part 1)
entry.content:
Business AI in ABAP Cloud – A Strategic Overview (Part 1)

Cheers ABAP folks!

If you've been anywhere near the SAP developer community recently, you've noticed that one topic keeps coming up in every conversation: AI. And with it, a question that many ABAP developers have been asking themselves — "Where does ABAP fit in an AI-driven world?"

The short answer: right at the center.

In the 2026 SAP Developer Insights Survey, ABAP remains the most widely used language in the SAP ecosystem at 82%. ABAP is not fading into the background. It is the technology backbone for SAP S/4HANA, SAP Integrated Business Planning, SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP Environment and with the ABAP Cloud development model, it is evolving to meet the demands of a cloud-native, AI-enabled future.

In this blog post, I want to give you a strategic overview of how Business AI capabilities are taking shape in ABAP Cloud: What's available today, what's on the roadmap, and how you can start building.

ABAP Cloud and AI — The Big Picture

Before we dive into the AI specifics, let's set the stage. ABAP Cloud supports a comprehensive set of development scenarios: From transactional SAP Fiori apps and embedded analytics, through process and data integration, to background processing and on-stack extensibility. The diagram below shows the full landscape, and you'll notice that Joule, SAP’s digital assistant, is explicitly part of the picture. Business AI is not a separate silo or an add-on. It is woven into the same architecture you already use for building ABAP Cloud applications with CDS entities and RAP Business Objects.

Figure 1: Joule integration in the ABAP Cloud development model

The Two Pillars: Embedded AI and Agentic AI

SAP's Business AI strategy in ABAP Cloud rests on two complementary pillars. The following diagram illustrates the overall strategy:

Figure 2: Business AI Strategy in ABAP Cloud

Embedded AI Capabilities in ABAP Cloud

Embedded AI refers to AI capabilities that run directly within your ABAP application. These are powered by the ABAP AI SDK, which provides the bare-metal functionalities, and the ABAP Cloud development model, which adds the integration, compliance, and UX layer on top.

Available and planned capabilities include:

  • Data Masking: Ensure privacy and compliance when sending data to AI models. Control what data leaves your system.
  • Document Extraction:  Extract structured information from unstructured documents directly within your ABAP processes.
  • Document Grounding: Provide domain-specific context to AI models so that responses are accurate and relevant to your business data.
  • Data Prediction with RAP Recommendations: Leverage prediction capabilities integrated into the RAP programming model to suggest field values, next actions, or classifications.
  • Human-in-the-Loop with RAP Notifications: Keep humans in control. AI can propose, but users confirm with notification-based workflows built into RAP.
  • Background Processing Framework: Run AI workloads asynchronously using the Background Processing Framework (bgPF), so that long-running AI tasks don't block your users.

The key advantage of Embedded AI is the seamless in-app experience. Your end users don't need to learn a new tool or change their workflow — AI capabilities surface right where they already work. 

Feel free to checkout the tutorial written by @jasmin_gruschke to jump start into the ABAP AI SDK.

 

Agentic AI Capabilities in SAP Business AI Platform

Agentic AI takes a different approach. Instead of embedding intelligence into a single application, it enables Joule and Agents to orchestrate across your business applications from the outside, through governed APIs.

The architecture supports:

  • Joule (broad-scope): SAP's digital assistant that can interact with your applications via natural language, performing the same tasks a user would.
  • Agents (narrow-scope): Specialised agents designed for specific, well-defined tasks with high automation potential.
  • Connectivity via OData, SQL, and MCP — Multiple integration paths ensure that Joule can reach your business logic regardless of how it's exposed.

Planned investments focus on ABAP side is on achieving unparalleled accuracy, generic API coverage across the application landscape, and enabling ECC environments, extending the reach of agentic AI beyond S/4HANA Cloud.

Ok, but when should I use what?

This is the question I get most often, and the honest answer is (like often in software development): it depends on the scenario, and in some cases, you'll want both.

Figure 3: Embedding AI vs. Agentic Orchestration

 

 

Embedded AI

Agentic AI via Joule

Development effort

Additional development required (ABAP AI SDK)

Remote service enablement required

Flexibility

Less flexible (model replacements, prompting bound to your code)

More flexible (orchestrated centrally)

User experience

Seamless, in-app, low entry barrier for end users

Natural language interaction via Joule, optimized via spaces concept in Joule Work.

Best for

Heavily used processes with high acceleration potential

Broad application coverage, high automation potential

My personal recommendation

  • If a process is used hundreds of times a day, every second counts and your active business users are used to an existing application: Embed AI directly into your application to see results fast.
  • If you want to enable your application landscape for AI-driven automation at scale, enable it for Joule. Be prepared to do this in the upcoming years for the most of your business processes.

Where can I find additional information?

If you would like to see an implementation of embedded AI in ABAP Cloud or the integration in Joule by using Joule capabilities in action, feel free to check out my recent Devtoberfest session on that. Watch it here:

 

Stay tuned for further blog posts, where we deep dive into the implementation details!

Cheerio ABAP Folks!

entry.title: A Battery Recall, a Graph, and an AI Agent
entry.content:
This is a personal portfolio project exploring graph capabilities of the SAP HANA database. It tries to answer two questions: can a graph find everyone affected by a motorcycle battery recall, and can an AI Agent make a sensible remedy plan when replacement battery packs are scarce.

 

I asked Claude Code (Opus 5.5) what would be a good showcase for a graph. He suggested we do a spike first: a quick, throwaway experiment to see whether an idea holds water before anyone builds anything.

 

Spike one: The where-used index

The first candidate was ABAP's own where-used index. Table WBCROSSGT has 9.7 million rows on my A4H, and as a graph of who uses which type it came to 205,145 vertices and 1,017,224 edges. Unknown depth, cycles, the lot. Surely a job for a graph?

Turns out, not really. A plain ABAP loop of about 25 lines (level by level, SELECT ... FOR ALL ENTRIES, a hashed table of what it had already seen) found exactly the same objects in all four test cases, within about 2 seconds and with no setup. Warm, the graph was 3 to 8 times faster, but building it cold took 7 to 14 seconds. And the one job that should have been its home turf, finding cycles, gave no answer after 9 minutes, so we aborted it.

So much for that.

 

Spike two: The real-life project

Then I remembered a project I once did.

  • A manufacturing component is found to be defective.
  • Find all production orders where it was used,
  • then find the subsequent production orders where the material produced in the previous one was used as a component (several levels deep),
  • then find the sales orders where it was sold,
  • then find out whether it was shipped to a customer or is still at a storage location.

The objective: notify the customer and send them a replacement, or take the product out of the storage location and scrap it.

Would that have been a good case for a graph? We had no data to try it on. So we invented some, and gave it a home in my Supply Chain Rescue demo app, which already has a fictional maker of electric motorcycles. Electric motorcycles have batteries. Batteries have cell lots. You can see where this is going.

A second spike on that idea went better, so we built the real thing: Recall Rescue.

 

The battery genealogy

Claude generated 12 weeks of motorcycle production and sales, from week 28 of 2026, with a battery genealogy behind every one of them:

  • a cell lot from the supplier VoltCell goes into battery modules,
  • modules go into packs,
  • packs go into motorcycles, or wait at the service stock as spare packs,
  • motorcycles go to customers, or wait at a plant, a dealer or the service stock.

That alone would be a tree: every module sits in one pack and every pack in one motorcycle, so from any module there is exactly one way forward. What breaks the simple tree is reuse and remanufacturing:

  • On 1 September, 8 private motorcycles from week 29 got a new pack.
  • Their old packs were taken apart, and 2 modules each from 2 old packs made one remanufactured pack.

So now a module has two links:

  1. the old one to the pack it came from,
  2. the new one to the remanufactured pack.

On 21 September, 3 of the remanufactured packs went into motorcycles sold in weeks 31 to 35, under warranty. The old links stay in the database as history, marked inactive, and that will matter in a minute.

A perfect setup to declare one lot defective and try to trace it.

Side note: the EU thinks along the same lines. From 18 February 2027 every LMT and electric vehicle battery placed on the EU market, electric motorcycle batteries included, needs a battery passport, and a remanufactured battery gets "a new battery passport linked to the battery passport or passports of the original battery or batteries" (Article 77 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542). Recall Rescue doesn't build passports, mind you, but the links behind them make a graph for the same reason the workshop does here.

 

All in all 27,814 items and 42,487 links in two Database Tables in A4H, generated from a fixed seed, so the world comes out the same every time.

 

Four lines of openCypher

If you haven't met openCypher yet: it's a query language for graphs, the open version of Cypher, which came from Neo4j. Where SQL makes you join tables, openCypher has you draw the pattern you're looking for, in ASCII art. (a) is a node, -[r]-> is a relationship pointing from one node to the next, and [*1..4] means 1 to 4 relationships, whatever lies in between (the part that takes a loop in ABAP).

  • MATCH draws the pattern,
  • WHERE filters it,
  • RETURN says what you want back.

HANA understands a subset of it and runs it against a graph workspace.

The question for a recall is: who has a battery with cells from this lot, right now? In openCypher it reads almost like the sentence (RETURN trimmed):

MATCH p = (l)-[*1..4]->(u), (u)-[h]->(t)
WHERE l.VERTEXID = 'LOT-VC-W29-03' AND (u.KIND = 'VIN' OR u.KIND = 'PACK') AND (t.KIND = 'CUST' OR t.KIND = 'SLOC')
  AND h.ACTIVE = 'X' AND ALL(e IN RELATIONSHIPS(p) WHERE e.ACTIVE = 'X')
RETURN u.VERTEXID AS UNIT, t.VERTEXID AS HOLDER

Start at the lot, follow 1 to 4 links to a motorcycle or a pack, then one more link to whoever holds it - a customer or a storage location. Current links only.

That last condition is important. For the lot LOT-VC-W29-03 the trace finds 27 units with their holders. Let it follow the history too, and it finds 35: Eight customers would get a recall notice for a battery that isn't in their motorcycle any more.

This is what the trace has to walk through: the whole family tree of LOT-VC-W29-03, straight from the vertex and edge tables, history and all. The red dashed links are the 8 packs the workshop took out, and the grey motorcycles are the 8 customers who would get a notice for nothing:

And this is what the four lines of openCypher make of it, as the app draws their answer: 27 units with their holders, 4 of them through the remanufactured packs, and not one of the 8 grey motorcycles:

How do I know the graph isn't just confidently wrong? Claude also wrote an oracle: a plain JavaScript walk over the same items and links, level by level, with no graph anywhere. For all 8 standard lots of week 29 the two agree exactly, unit by unit and holder by holder.

And speed? Doesn't matter at this size. In the spike the ABAP loop took 77 ms and the graph 67 ms. Now a warm trace answers in about 400 to 800 ms, through OData and all. Here is a screenshot from Postman:

 

The catch

There is one, and it's big if you live in ABAP Cloud.

  • The trace runs on A4H's own HANA, over a graph workspace that an AMDP method defines on two CDS view entities.
  • But openCypher won't go through an AMDP. ABAP's check rejects the SQL that HANA expands the query into: "The ABAP database schema ... cannot be specified explicitly". Uwe Fetzer ( @UweFetzer_se38 ) reported exactly this back in 2019, in his SAP Community question Opencypher in AMDP, and SAP called it a bug. I hit the same error on my release 816 system.
  • What does work is native SQL through ADBC (cl_sql_statement): SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE ... QUERY '...' ). ADBC is not released for ABAP Cloud, so this is classic ABAP only.
  • No query parameters either. The lot goes into the query text, so it's checked against a strict pattern first, and nothing but a lot number of the form LOT-VC-W29-03 gets through.
  • HANA 2.00.087 speaks a subset of openCypher: no named variable-length edge like [e*1..4], and one hop per pattern element. Hence the comma in the MATCH above.

The trace is a RAP custom entity, so to everyone else it's just another OData entity set.

 

Inside ZCL_RR_TRACE

The whole graph part lives in one class, ZCL_RR_TRACE. The graph itself is ten lines of it, an AMDP method that says which CDS view entity holds the vertices and which the edges:

METHOD graph BY DATABASE GRAPH WORKSPACE FOR HDB
  LANGUAGE SQL
  USING zi_rr_graphedge zi_rr_graphvertex.
  edge table zi_rr_graphedge
    source column sourceid
    target column targetid
    key    column edgeid
  vertex table zi_rr_graphvertex
    key    column vertexid
ENDMETHOD.

ZI_RR_GraphVertex reads the items, ZI_RR_GraphEdge the links. No copy of the data, no extra tables. Apart from that, the class does three jobs:

  1. It wakes the graph up. HANA creates an AMDP graph workspace only the first time an AMDP uses it, and our query comes in through ADBC. So before every query a tiny GraphScript procedure (HANA's own graph language) counts the vertices. The count goes nowhere - it's the wake-up call.
