entry.title: Building a RAP Managed Business Object on SAP BTP — A Complete Step-by-Step Guide
entry.content:
SAP RAP Managed Scenario — Step-by-Step Guide

                         A complete, beginner-friendly implementation of an SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) Managed Business Object — built on SAP BTP ABAP Environment Trial. This repository walks through every layer of the RAP stack from database tables to the Fiori Elements UI, with detailed explanations of why each artifact exists, not just how to create it.

Table of Contents

  • Overview
  • Architecture
  • Prerequisites
  • Step 1 — Database Table
  • Step 2 — Draft Table
  • Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I)
  • Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C)
  • Step 5 — Metadata Extension
  • Step 6 — Behavior Definition (Interface)
  • Step 7 — Behavior Definition (Projection)
  • Step 8 — Behavior Implementation
  • Step 9 — Service Definition & Binding
  • Key Takeaways

 

Overview
What is RAP?
                         The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) is SAP's modern, cloud-ready framework for building transactional Fiori applications in ABAP Cloud. It replaces older approaches like BOPF and classic ABAP MVC, and is the standard for SAP S/4HANA Cloud and BTP ABAP Environment development.
 
RAP provides:
  • A structured, layered architecture from database to UI
  • Built-in OData service generation (no manual SEGW needed)
  • Framework-managed CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete)
  • Draft handling for save/resume workflows
  • Clean Core compliance — no modifications to SAP standard objects

What is the Managed Scenario?

TypeWho handles CRUD?When to use
ManagedRAP Framework automaticallyNew custom BOs — no legacy dependencies
UnmanagedDeveloper writes all logicWrapping legacy function modules / BAPIs

In the Managed scenario, the RAP framework automatically handles database INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT operations. You only write code for custom business logic like validations, determinations, and custom actions. This makes it the fastest and cleanest way to build a new Business Object from scratch.

 

  Architecture

The RAP stack follows a strict layered architecture. Each layer has a specific responsibility, and no layer should skip or bypass another.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                            Fiori Elements UI                                                                    │
│                                                                   (Auto-generated from OData)                                                      │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │ OData V4
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                           Service Definition + Service Binding                                                                   │
│                                       (Exposes which entities go into OData)                                                                 │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                          PROJECTION LAYER (ZC_*)                                                                   │
│                                    CDS Consumption View + Projection Behavior Def.                                              │
│                                   (Service-specific: UI annotations, field exposure)                                                  │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │ as projection on
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                   INTERFACE LAYER (ZR_* / ZI_*)                                                                   │
│                                       CDS Interface View + Base Behavior Definition                                                   │
│                                        (Service-agnostic: data model, business logic)                                                  │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                              │
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                 DATABASE LAYER                                                                               │
│                                                    Main Table (ZDB_*) + Draft Table (*_D)                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • SAP BTP Trial account — 
  • Steps to create Trial account 
  • ABAP Environment trial instance provisioned on BTP 
  • Eclipse IDE with ABAP Development Tools (ADT) plugin installed 
  • Connected to your BTP ABAP system via ADT
  • Basic understanding of ABAP syntax and CDS views

Step 1 — Database Table (Main Table)

What is it?

The database table is the foundation of your Business Object. It is the actual physical table in the SAP HANA database where all your application data is permanently stored. Every field you want to persist — travel ID, agency, customer, price, status — must be defined here first.

Why do we create it?

Without a database table, there is no place to store data. The entire RAP stack above it — CDS views, behavior definitions, OData services — are all abstractions built on top of this table. The table is the single source of truth for your BO's data.

Structure of a RAP-compliant database table

A RAP managed table must follow specific conventions:

@EndUserText.label : 'Products'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #RESTRICTED
define table znk_t_product {

  key client            : abap.clnt not null;
  key pro_uuid          : sysuuid_x16 not null;
  key product_id        : abap.char(10) not null;
  description           : abap.char(40);
  @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'znk_t_product.uom'
  qty                   : abap.quan(8,3);
  uom                   : abap.unit(3);
  @Semantics.amount.currencyCode : 'znk_t_product.currency'
  price                 : abap.curr(15,2);
  currency              : abap.cuky;
  mfg_date              : abap.datn;
  exp_date              : abap.datn;
  validdays             : abap.int4;
  plant                 : abap.char(4);
  local_created_by      : abp_creation_user;
  local_created_at      : abp_creation_tstmpl;
  local_last_changed_by : abp_locinst_lastchange_user;
  local_last_changed_at : abp_locinst_lastchange_tstmpl;
  last_changed_at       : abp_lastchange_tstmpl;

}

Important: The last_changed_at field with type abp_lastchange_tstmpl is critical for the ETag mechanism. When two users try to update the same record simultaneously, RAP compares this timestamp to detect conflicts and reject stale updates.

Key fields explained

FieldTypePurpose

clientabap.clntSAP client field — mandatory first key in every table
product_idBusiness keyUnique identifier for each product record
local_created_byy / local_created_atAdmin fieldsAuto-populated by RAP framework — track who created the record
local_last_changed_by / local_last_changed_atAdmin fieldsAuto-populated — track last modifier
last_changed_atETag fieldUsed by RAP for optimistic locking / concurrency control

 

Step 2 — Draft Table (Why It Exists)

What is a Draft Table?

The draft table is a temporary storage table where incomplete, unsaved data is held while a user is still filling in a form. It has an identical structure to your main database table, with some additional draft-specific fields added by the framework.

By convention, draft tables are named the same as the main table with a _D suffix:

Main table   : ZNK_T_PRODUCT        ← permanent, saved data
Draft table  : ZNK_T_PRODUCT_D      ← temporary, in-progress data
 

Why do we need a Draft Table?

Imagine a user opens a "Create Product" form in a Fiori app and starts filling in the fields — Plant, UOM, MFG & Exp dates. Halfway through, their browser crashes, or they need to attend a meeting. Without draft handling, all their work is lost.

With Draft Handling:

User opens form
      │
      ▼
Data saved to DRAFT TABLE immediately (auto-save)
      │
      ├── User continues tomorrow → draft is still there ✅
      ├── User switches device → draft is still there ✅
      └── User clicks "Save" → data moves to MAIN TABLE ✅
                               draft record is deleted ✅
 

The draft table ensures no data loss during long-running create/edit operations. It also enables the "Edit" button behavior in Fiori apps — when you click Edit on a saved record, RAP copies the record to the draft table so your edits don't affect the live data until you explicitly save.

How to define the Draft Table

You don't write the draft table manually field by field. You reference it in your Behavior Definition and let ADT generate it:

-- In your Behavior Definition:
managed implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;
strict ( 2 );
with draft;
define behavior for znk_product_I //alias <alias_name>
persistent table znk_t_product               -- ← your main table
draft table znk_t_product_d                  -- ← your draft table (RAP manages this)            
...
 

When you activate the behavior definition, ADT automatically creates the draft table with the correct structure.

Draft Table vs Main Table — Side by Side

AspectMain TableDraft Table
PurposePermanent business dataTemporary in-progress data
When data lands hereOn "Save" actionOn every field change (auto-save)
Who can see itAll usersOnly the user editing
Deleted whenNever (business record)On Save or Discard
NamedZNK_T_PRODUCTZNK_T_PRODUCT_D
Created byDeveloper manuallyADT generates from BDEF
 
 
     Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I)

What is the Interface View?

The Interface View is the base CDS View Entity that sits directly on top of your database table. It forms the service-agnostic data model of your Business Object — meaning it defines the complete data structure without any UI-specific concerns.

By convention, Interface Views are prefixed with ZR_ (R = Root) for root entities or ZI_ (I = Interface).

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Product Interface View'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define root view entity znk_product_I as select from znk_t_product
association [0..1] to I_Currency as _Currency on $projection.Currency = _Currency.Currency
association [ 0..1] to I_UnitOfMeasure as _Uom on $projection.Uom = _Uom.UnitOfMeasure

{
    key pro_uuid as ProUuid,
    key product_id as ProductId,
    description as Description,
    @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'uom'
    qty as Qty,
    @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
    entity.name: 'I_UnitOfMeasure',
    entity.element: 'UnitOfMeasure',
    useForValidation: true
     }]
    uom as Uom,
    @Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'currency'
    price as Price,
    @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
    entity.name: 'I_Currency',
    entity.element: 'Currency',
    useForValidation: true
     }]
    currency as Currency,
    mfg_date as MfgDate,
    exp_date as ExpDate,
    plant as Plant,
    validdays as ValidDays,
    @Semantics.user.createdBy: true
    local_created_by as LocalCreatedBy,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.createdAt: true
    local_created_at as LocalCreatedAt,
    @Semantics.user.lastChangedBy: true
    local_last_changed_by as LocalLastChangedBy,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.localInstanceLastChangedAt: true
    local_last_changed_at as LocalLastChangedAt,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.lastChangedAt: true
    last_changed_at as LastChangedAt,
    _Uom as UomDetails,
    _Currency as CurrencyDetails
     // Make association public
}

Why do we need the Interface View?

The Interface View serves several critical purposes:

1. Abstraction from the database table The database table uses technical field names and types. The Interface View can rename, cast, and join fields into a cleaner business model. If the table structure changes, only the interface view needs to be updated — everything above is unaffected.

2. It is the root of the composition tree The keyword define root view entity declares this as the top of a Business Object hierarchy. All child entities (like Booking under Travel) are connected back to this root via COMPOSITION OF associations.

3. It is reusable across multiple services The interface view has NO UI annotations, NO Fiori-specific logic. This means the same interface view can power:

  • A Fiori Elements app (via projection view → OData)
  • A remote API (via a different projection)

4. Associations are defined here Associations to related entities (Currency, UnitOfMeasure) are defined on the interface view so they are available to all Products.

The define root view entity keyword

This keyword does two important things:

  • It declares this CDS view as a Root Entity of a Business Object
  • It enables it to have its own Behavior Definition repository object
  • Only root entities can define composition of child associations
  Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C)

What is the Consumption View?

The Consumption View (also called the Projection View) sits on top of the Interface View and represents a service-specific, tailored window into the Business Object. It is what gets exposed to the outside world — via OData, via a Fiori app, via an API.

By convention, Consumption Views are prefixed or suffixed with ZC_ (C = Consumption).

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Product Consumption View'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true
define root view entity znk_product_c
  provider contract transactional_query as projection on znk_product_I                           -- ← the key syntax: "as projection on"
  association [1..1] to znk_product_I as _BaseEntity on $projection.ProUuid = _BaseEntity.ProUuid
                                                    and $projection.ProductId = _BaseEntity.ProductId
{
key ProUuid,
key ProductId,
Description,
@Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'Uom'
Qty,
@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition:[{ entity:{ name: 'I_UnitOfMeasure',
                                             element: 'UnitOfMeasure'},
                                    useForValidation: true }]
Uom,
@Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'Currency'
Price,
@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ entity:{ name: 'I_Currency',
                                     element: 'Currency' },
                                     useForValidation: true  }]
Currency,
MfgDate,
ExpDate,
Plant,
ValidDays,
LocalCreatedBy,
LocalCreatedAt,
LocalLastChangedBy,
LocalLastChangedAt,
LastChangedAt,
/* Associations */
UomDetails,
CurrencyDetails,
_BaseEntity
}
 

Why do we need the Consumption View if we already have the Interface View?

This is the most common question from beginners. The answer is separation of concerns:

 
Concern Interface View✅Consumption View
Business data model✅Defined hereInherited from interface
Associations & compositions✅Defined hereRedirected here
UI annotations (@UI.*)❌Not here✅Via Metadata Extension
Value helps (@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition)❌Not here✅Defined here
Field aliasing for UI❌Not here✅Can rename fields
Access control✅Defined hereAdditional checks possible
Which fields to exposeAll fieldsSubset — only what the app needs

Real-world analogy:             

                       Think of the Interface View as a master employee record with every piece of data. The Consumption View is a role-specific form an HR manager sees salary and personal data, a project manager sees only skills and availability. Same underlying data, different projections.

The as projection on syntax

This is what makes a view a projection view. It tells the RAP framework:

  • "This view is consuming/projecting another view"
  • "The underlying BO's behavior definition applies through here"
  • "Compositions must be redirected to their own projection equivalents"

🎨Step 5 — Metadata Extension

What is a Metadata Extension?

A Metadata Extension (.ddlx file) is a separate repository object that holds UI annotations for a CDS view, kept completely separate from the view's data model definition. It is applied on top of a Consumption View that has @Metadata.allowExtensions: true.

@Metadata.layer: #CORE
@UI.headerInfo: { typeName: 'Product', typeNamePlural: 'Products' }
annotate entity znk_product_c with
{

@UI.facet: [{ id: 'Info',
              type: #IDENTIFICATION_REFERENCE,
              label: 'Product',
              position: 10}]
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 10, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH,hidden: true},
                   { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'checkProductValidity', label: 'Check Validity', position: 10 ,emphasized: true},              --- Custom Button Added Here 
                   { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'clearValidDays',       label: 'Clear',          position: 20 ,emphasized: true}],             --- Custom Button Added Here   
        identification: [{position: 10, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true},
                         { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'checkProductValidity', label: 'Check Validity', position: 10 }] }
  ProUuid;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 20, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 20, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 10  }] }
  ProductId;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 30, label: 'Description', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 30, label: 'Description', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 30  }] }
  Description;
   @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 31, label: 'Qty', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 31, label: 'Quantity', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Qty;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 40, label: 'UOM', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 40, label: 'Unit Of Measurement', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  Uom;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 50, label: 'Price', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 50, label: 'Price', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Price;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 60, label: 'Currency', importance: #HIGH,hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 60, label: 'Currency', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  Currency;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 70, label: 'MFG Date', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 70, label: 'Manufacture Date', importance: #HIGH}] }
  MfgDate;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 80, label: 'Exp. Date', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 80, label: 'Expiry Date', importance: #HIGH}] }
  ExpDate;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 90, label: 'Plant', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 90, label: 'Plant', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Plant;
   @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 91, label: 'Valid Days', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 91, label: 'Valid Days', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 91  }] }
  ValidDays;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 100, label: 'Created By', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 100, label: 'Created By', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalCreatedBy;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 110, label: 'Created At', importance: #HIGH }],
        identification: [{position: 110, label: 'Created At', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalCreatedAt;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 120, label: 'Last Changed By', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true }],
        identification: [{position: 120, label: 'Last Changed By', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalLastChangedBy;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 130, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 130, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalLastChangedAt;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 140, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 140, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  LastChangedAt;

}
 

Why do we use a Metadata Extension instead of putting annotations directly in the CDS view?

There are three powerful reasons:

1. Clean Separation of Concerns The CDS view defines WHAT data exists. The Metadata Extension defines HOW it looks in the UI. Mixing both in one file creates a massive, hard-to-read view definition. Separating them keeps each file focused and maintainable.

2. Extensibility (Key User / Partner / Customer layers) The @Metadata.layer annotation supports a hierarchy:

#CORE          ← SAP / developer defines base UI
#CUSTOMER      ← Customer adds their annotations
#PARTNER       ← Relates to a partner extension of a product 
#INDUSTRY      ← Relates to an industry-specific extension of a product (SAP Industry Solution)
 

Lower layers can be overridden by higher layers without modifying the original files. This is the foundation of SAP's extensibility model.

3. Keeps the CDS View Clean for Multiple Consumers If you put @UI.lineItem directly in the CDS view, those annotations are baked in for everyone. With a metadata extension, different services can have different metadata extensions on the same projection view — different UI layouts for different apps.

Common UI Annotations in Metadata Extensions

 
AnnotationPurposeExample
@UI.lineItemShow field in the list tableList page columns
@UI.identificationShow field in the detail formObject page fields
@UI.selectionFieldShow field in the filter barSearch filters
@UI.facetDefine sections/tabs on the object page"Product Details" tab
@UI.hiddenHide field from UI entirelyInternal fields
@UI.dataActionAdd a button for a custom action"Valid Days" button

⚙️Step 6 — Behavior Definition (Interface View)

What is a Behavior Definition?

A Behavior Definition (BDEF) is a repository object that defines what operations are allowed on a Business Object. It answers questions like:

  • Can this BO be created, updated, deleted?
  • Which fields are read-only or mandatory?
  • Does it support draft handling?
  • What custom actions exist (like "Valid Days")?
  • How are primary keys generated?

Interface View Behavior Definition

The base BDEF sits on the Interface View and defines the complete set of capabilities of the BO:

managed implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;
strict ( 2 );
with draft;
define behavior for znk_product_I //alias <alias_name>
persistent table znk_t_product
draft table znk_t_product_d
lock master                                                         -- Locking mechanism
total etag LastChangedAt
authorization master ( global )
etag master LastChangedAt                                           -- ETag for concurrency control
{

 -- Field controls
 field ( mandatory : create ) ProductId;                            -- Makes Mandatory when create
 field ( readonly )                                                 -- Makes non-editable
 LocalCreatedAt,
 LocalCreatedBy,
 LocalLastChangedAt,
 LocalLastChangedBy,
 LastChangedAt;
 field ( numbering : managed ) ProUuid;                             -- Makes Numbering Managed
 field ( readonly : update ) ProUuid, ProductId;                    -- Makes non-editable when update

   -- Standard CRUD operations (framework handles automatically in managed)
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  -- Custom actions (developer implements)
  action  ( features : instance ) checkProductValidity result [1] $self;
  action  ( features : instance ) clearValidDays result [1] $self;

  -- Draft related Actions
  draft action Edit;
  draft action Activate optimized;
  draft action Discard;
  draft action Resume;
  draft determine action Prepare;

  -- Mapping is very important to store the values to DB 
  mapping for znk_t_product
    {
      ProUuid            = pro_uuid;
      ProductId          = product_id;
      Description        = description;
      Qty                = qty;
      Uom                = uom;
      Price              = price;
      Currency           = currency;
      MfgDate            = mfg_date;
      ExpDate            = exp_date;
      Plant              = plant;
      ValidDays          = validdays;
      LocalCreatedBy     = local_created_by;
      LocalCreatedAt     = local_created_at;
      LocalLastChangedAt = local_last_changed_at;
      LocalLastChangedBy = local_last_changed_by;
      LastChangedAt      = last_changed_at;
    }
}
 

Key BDEF keywords explained

managed — Tells the RAP framework to auto-handle all database operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). You don't write any MODIFY dbtab statements yourself.

with draft — Activates the draft handling mechanism. The framework will use your draft table for all in-progress changes.

etag master LocalLastChangedAt — Enables optimistic locking. Before any update, RAP compares the LocalLastChangedAt timestamp in the request with the database to detect if someone else modified the record in between.

lock master — When a user starts editing (enters draft mode), the record is locked so no other user can simultaneously edit the same record.

numbering:managed — (when used on a field) Tells the framework to auto-generate a UUID primary key at CREATE time — no manual key assignment needed.

validation — A method you implement in the Behavior Implementation class. Called by the framework before save. Return error messages to block the save.

determination — A method that auto-runs when specific fields change. Used for defaulting values (e.g., set status to "Open" when a Product is created).

action — A custom operation beyond standard CRUD. Adds a button in the Fiori UI. Example: "Valid Days" changes status to Accepted.

🔒Step 7 — Behavior Definition (Projection View)

What is the Projection Behavior Definition?

The Projection BDEF sits on the Consumption View and exposes a subset of the base BDEF's operations for a specific service. It acts as a gatekeeper — you decide which operations this particular OData service gets to offer.

projection;
strict ( 2 );
use draft;

define behavior for znk_product_c //alias <alias_name>
{
  use create;                           -- Expose create to this service
  use update;                           -- Expose update to this service
  use delete;                           -- Expose delete to this service

  use action Edit;
  use action Activate;
  use action Discard;
  use action Prepare;
  use action Resume;


  -- Expose only the custom actions this service needs
  use action checkProductValidity;
  use action clearValidDays;
}
 

Interface BDEF vs Projection BDEF — Why both?

    
 Interface BDEFProjection BDEF
Sits onInterface View (Z*_R)Consumption View (Z*_C)
ContainsALL possible operationsSUBSET for this service
ImplementationDeveloper writes code hereJust use statements — no code
ReusabilityOne per BOOne per service/app
AnalogyFull employee recordRole-specific access form

Imagine you have two apps using the same Travel BO:

  • Admin App → projection BDEF exposes: create, update, delete, ValidDays, Clear
  • Read-Only Report App → projection BDEF exposes: nothing (read-only by omission)

Same base BO, completely different service behavior — controlled purely by the projection BDEF.

💻Step 8 — Behavior Implementation (BAP)

What is the Behavior Implementation?

The Behavior Implementation is an ABAP class that contains the actual code for all custom operations defined in the base Behavior Definition — validations, determinations, and actions. In managed scenarios, you do NOT write code for standard CRUD — the framework handles that. You only write code for your custom business logic.

The class is named in the BDEF with implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;.

"! <p class="shorttext synchronized" lang="en">Behavior Implementation for ZNK_PRODUCT_I</p>
CLASS zbp_nk_product_i DEFINITION PUBLIC ABSTRACT FINAL FOR BEHAVIOR OF znk_product_i.
ENDCLASS.

CLASS zbp_nk_product_i IMPLEMENTATION.
ENDCLASS.
 

The actual logic sits in local classes inside the implementation class's .locals_imp include:

Validation Example — validateDates

CLASS lhc_znk_product_I DEFINITION INHERITING FROM cl_abap_behavior_handler.
  PRIVATE SECTION.
    METHODS get_global_authorizations FOR GLOBAL AUTHORIZATION
    REQUEST requested_authorizations FOR znk_product_I RESULT result.
    METHODS checkProductValidity FOR MODIFY
       keys FOR ACTION znk_product_I~checkProductValidity RESULT result.
    METHODS get_instance_features FOR INSTANCE FEATURES
      keys REQUEST requested_features FOR znk_product_I RESULT result.
    METHODS clearvaliddays FOR MODIFY
       keys FOR ACTION znk_product_i~clearvaliddays RESULT result.
ENDCLASS.

CLASS lhc_znk_product_I IMPLEMENTATION.
  METHOD get_global_authorizations.
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD checkProductValidity.

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE                               --Read entries from Interface view to lt_products
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE                             --Modify entries from Interface view to lt_products
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = CONV i( ls-ExpDate - ls-MfgDate )
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    LOOP AT lt_products INTO DATA(ls_product).                                  --Validation on to lt_products
      IF ls_product-ExpDate <= ls_product-MfgDate.
        APPEND VALUE #(
          %tky = ls_product-%tky
          %msg = new_message_with_text(
                   severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                   text     = 'Expiry Date must be after Manufacturing Date!' )
        ) TO reported-znk_product_i.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                                   ENTITY znk_product_I
                                   ALL FIELDS
                                   WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                                   RESULT DATA(lt_result).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result                                        --Return the modified entries to result
                      ( %tky   = ls-%tky
                        %param = ls ) ).   

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD get_instance_features.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
     ENTITY znk_product_I
     FIELDS ( ProductId )
     WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
     RESULT DATA(lt_products)
     FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_products
                      ( %tky                          = ls-%tky
                        %action-checkProductValidity  = if_abap_behv=>fc-o-enabled ) ).
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD clearValidDays.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = 0
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                      ENTITY znk_product_I
                      ALL FIELDS
                      WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                      RESULT DATA(lt_result).
    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result
        ( %tky   = ls-%tky
          %param = ls ) ).   
  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.
 

Determination Example — setInitialStatus

METHOD setInitialStatus.
  " Read travels that were just created
  READ ENTITIES OF zr_traveltp IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Travel
      FIELDS ( OverallStatus )
      WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_travel)
    FAILED failed.

  " Filter: only set status if it's initial (empty)
  DELETE lt_travel WHERE OverallStatus IS NOT INITIAL.
  CHECK lt_travel IS NOT INITIAL.

  " Set default status to 'Open'
  MODIFY ENTITIES OF zr_traveltp IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Travel
      UPDATE FIELDS ( OverallStatus )
      WITH VALUE #( FOR ls_travel IN lt_travel (
        %tky          = ls_travel-%tky
        OverallStatus = 'O'   " O = Open
      ) )
    REPORTED DATA(lt_reported).

  reported = CORRESPONDING #( DEEP lt_reported ).
ENDMETHOD.
 

Action Example — checkProductValidity

METHOD checkProductValidity.

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = CONV i( ls-ExpDate - ls-MfgDate )
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    LOOP AT lt_products INTO DATA(ls_product).
      IF ls_product-ExpDate <= ls_product-MfgDate.
        APPEND VALUE #(
          %tky = ls_product-%tky
          %msg = new_message_with_text(
                   severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                   text     = 'Expiry Date must be after Manufacturing Date!' )
        ) TO reported-znk_product_i.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                                   ENTITY znk_product_I
                                   ALL FIELDS
                                   WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                                   RESULT DATA(lt_result).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result
                      ( %tky   = ls-%tky
                        %param = ls ) ).   

  ENDMETHOD.
 

Important RAP-specific ABAP concepts

READ ENTITIES — The RAP-specific way to read data from a BO. Always use this inside behavior implementations — never use SELECT directly.

MODIFY ENTITIES — The RAP-specific way to change data inside behavior implementations — never use MODIFY dbtab directly.

IN LOCAL MODE — Bypasses authorization checks and feature controls when called from within the same BO's implementation. Important for internal BO operations.

%tky — The transactional key — a structure containing all key fields of the entity. Used to identify records throughout RAP's internal processing.

failed / reported — Standard output parameters for all RAP methods. Populate failed to signal which records errored. Populate reported to send messages back to the UI.

🌐Step 9 — Service Definition & Service Binding

Service Definition

Defines which CDS entities are exposed and under what names:

@EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for Consumption view'
define service Znk_sd_product {
  expose znk_product_c;
}
 

Service Binding

The Service Binding ties a Service Definition to a specific protocol and usage type. For Fiori apps, you create an OData V4 binding with type UI:

  • Binding Type: OData V4 - UI
  • Activate the binding to get the OData service URL
  • Use "Preview" in ADT to open the Fiori Elements app directly

Once activated, your Product BO is fully functional as a Fiori Elements List Report + Object Page app — with list, filter, create, edit, draft, save, and all your custom actions.

💡Key Takeaways

The Purpose of Each Layer — Summary

DATABASE TABLE     → Where data lives permanently
DRAFT TABLE        → Where in-progress data lives temporarily
INTERFACE VIEW     → Clean data model, service-agnostic, reusable
CONSUMPTION VIEW   → Service-specific window — what this app sees
METADATA EXTENSION → UI layout — how fields look in Fiori
BASE BDEF          → All possible BO operations defined
PROJECTION BDEF    → Subset of operations for this specific service
BAP CLASS          → Custom business logic — validations, actions
SERVICE DEFINITION → Which entities go into the OData service
SERVICE BINDING    → Which protocol (OData V4) and port (UI/API)
 

The Two-Layer Pattern (Interface + Consumption) — Why it matters

The separation of Interface and Consumption layers is the most important design decision in RAP. It gives you:

  1. Reusability — one BO, multiple services (UI service, API service, integration service)
  2. Flexibility — each service exposes exactly what it needs
  3. Stability — changing the UI doesn't break the underlying BO contract
  4. Extensibility — SAP's own S/4HANA BOs follow this same pattern

Managed vs Unmanaged at a glance

In this managed scenario, the RAP framework wrote all the database interaction code for you. You only wrote:

  • Validation logic (validateDates)
  • Determination logic (setInitialStatus)
  • Action logic (checkProductValidity, Clear)

Everything else — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, draft handling, locking, ETag — was handled by the framework automatically.

Github Link :  RAP-Managed-in-SAP 

Thanks,

Naveen Kumar SAP ABAP Developer | BTP Explorer

entry.title: The standalone app — exploring supplier recommendations with RAP + Fiori Elements
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 3 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". Part 1: the in‑transaction assistant (ME51N). Part 2: the SAP BTP + AI Core "brain". This part: the standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

TL;DR

Same AI, different doorway. In Part 1 the SAP AI Core recommendation lived inside ME51N — the buyer's in‑flow surface. But sometimes you want to step back and explore with the AI: compare suppliers across a whole basket of materials, let the model reason about whether one vendor can cover everything (one PO) or not (several), and tune the sourcing strategy. That's what this standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app does — the same guarded‑LLM engine as Part 1 and Part 2, wrapped in an interactive UI. It's a managed, draft‑enabled business object exposed as an OData V4 UI service, with one action, RankSuppliers, that orchestrates the AI recommendation end to end.

ranked suppliers and the sourcing scenario for a basket of materials

Two surfaces, one engine

Part 1's ME51N assistant is about flow — you're creating a requisition and the best vendor should just be there. This app is about exploration — a buyer or category manager asks, "for these five materials, what's the smartest way to source them?" Same KPIs, same guarded LLM, same validation — but here the answer includes a sourcing scenario across materials, not just a per‑line default.

  ME51N assistant (Part 1) Standalone app (this part)

Mindsetin‑flow, one line at a timeexplore a whole basket
Triggertyping a material in the PRcreate a Run, add materials, press Rank Suppliers
OutputDesired Vendor default + top‑5 popupranked suppliers + COMMON/SPLIT sourcing
Built withclassic BAdIRAP (managed BO) + Fiori Elements

The run header shows the sourcing scenario; items show the ranked suppliers

Annotated object page of a recommendation run

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “Wrapping up the series”.

The business object

It's a two‑level managed, draft‑enabled RAP BO:

  • Run (root) — one recommendation run: the consolidation preference, and after ranking, the scenario type, supplier count (= number of POs), coverage %, and AI status.
  • Item (child) — the materials in the run and, after ranking, each material's recommended supplier, reason, and confidence.

Interface CDS (ZI_VENDORREC_RUN / ZI_VENDORREC_ITEM) model the composition; projection CDS (ZC_VENDORREC_RUN / ZC_VENDORREC_ITEM) add the Fiori UI annotations; a service definition + OData V4 UI binding expose it to Fiori Elements. A material value help (ZI_VENDORREC_MAT_VH) gives an F4 that auto‑fills description/plant/group.

Managed draft BO exposed as an OData V4 UI service

One action does the orchestration

The whole recommendation is a single RAP action on the Run — RankSuppliers. Its handler reads the run's items, builds one candidate request per material (via the deterministic engine from Part 2), calls the service once for the whole run (so it can reason about consolidation), then writes the picks back onto the items and the scenario onto the header (handler trimmed for brevity):

METHOD rank_suppliers.
  " Deterministic engine (candidates/KPIs) + thin AI client (calls the BTP service)
  DATA(svc) = NEW zcl_vendorrec_service( ).
  DATA(ai)  = NEW zcl_vendorrec_ai_core( iv_destination = 'Z_VENDORREC_API' ).

  READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Run FIELDS ( ConsolidationPref ) WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys ) RESULT DATA(lt_runs).

  LOOP AT lt_runs INTO DATA(ls_run).
    " read this run's materials
    READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
      ENTITY Run BY \_Item FIELDS ( Material ) WITH VALUE #( ( %tky = ls_run-%tky ) ) RESULT DATA(lt_items).

    " one candidate request per material (KPIs computed deterministically in ABAP)
    DATA lt_req TYPE zcl_vendorrec_ai_core=>tt_llm_request.
    CLEAR lt_req.
    LOOP AT lt_items INTO DATA(ls_item).
      APPEND svc->build_llm_request( iv_material = ls_item-Material ) TO lt_req.
    ENDLOOP.

    " one call for the whole run -> honors the consolidation preference (COMMON/SPLIT)
    DATA(res) = ai->get_recommendation( it_requests = lt_req
                                        iv_consolidation_preference = ls_run-ConsolidationPref ).

    " write the recommendation back onto each item …
    " … and the scenario summary (type, #POs, coverage, AI status) onto the run header
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

Two things to note: the deterministic KPIs are computed in ABAP (nothing sensitive leaves S/4), and the sourcing scenario is derived server‑side, not by the LLM — exactly the guardrails from Part 2, reused unchanged.

Why RAP here, but a BAdI in ME51N?

Different jobs, different tools. ME51N already exists and the buyer is in it — enhancing it with a BAdI is the least‑intrusive way to add a default. This app is a new object with its own persistence, draft handling, and UI — which is exactly what RAP + Fiori Elements gives you almost for free (draft, locking, OData, List Report/Object Page). Same engine underneath; the right delivery vehicle for each context.

Consolidation preference: the buyer's strategy lever

The Run header carries a consolidation preference dropdown — CONSOLIDATE, BALANCED, BEST_FIT — which flows into the service call and steers the COMMON‑vs‑SPLIT decision (see Part 2). It's the one knob that lets a human set sourcing strategy while the AI does the reasoning: e.g. "prefer one supplier for the whole basket even at a small KPI cost," vs "give me the strongest supplier per material regardless."



Consolidation preference dropdown and the resulting sourcing scenario

Wrapping up the series

Across three parts we built one idea two ways, on one trustworthy engine:

  • Part 1 — ME51N: the recommendation in flow, defaulted into Desired Vendor with an explainable popup, via a supported BAdI.
  • Part 2 — BTP + AI Core: the guarded brain — deterministic KPIs in ABAP, an LLM kept honest by server‑side validation, secure S/4→BTP→AI Core connectivity, and no data leaving S/4 beyond KPIs.
  • Part 3 — RAP + Fiori: the explore surface — a managed draft BO that ranks suppliers across a basket and proposes the sourcing scenario.

The throughline is responsible, custom S/4HANA AI: deterministic where it must be, AI where it adds value, explainable and human‑in‑the‑loop throughout — built on SAP's own AI platform.

Where next? Extending the same pattern to purchase orders (ME21N), adding a price dimension, and turning the decision log into an adoption dashboard are the obvious next steps.

Thanks for reading the series. If you build something with this pattern — or take it somewhere we didn't — we'd genuinely like to hear about it in the comments.

entry.title: My First SAP RAP Application: Building a Student Management App Using Managed RAP
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community! 👋

In this blog post, I would like to share my hands-on experience building my first application using the SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

As part of my learning journey, I developed a simple Student Management Application using Managed RAP, ABAP CDS View Entities, OData V2, and SAP Fiori Elements.

The main objective was to understand how the different RAP development artifacts work together to build a transactional application.

The application supports standard CRUD operations:

  • Create — Add new students.

  • Read — Display existing student records.

  • Update — Modify student information.

  • Delete — Remove student records.

In this tutorial, I'll explain each development step, share the code, and discuss some challenges I encountered.

My Personal Experience

I started this project with a simple Managed RAP application that supported basic CRUD operations.

As I continued practicing in Eclipse and testing the application with SAP Fiori Elements, I wanted to understand how RAP handles real business requirements.

One of the most useful parts of the project was implementing Draft Handling. I initially encountered an error because the draft persistence table was not configured correctly. After resolving it, I tested the application by creating a student, leaving the page without activating the record, and returning to find my draft still available.

I also enjoyed implementing the Approve Student action and seeing the student status change from NEW to APPROVED directly in Fiori.

Working through these steps helped me understand RAP much better than simply reading about its features.

AI disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help structure and draft parts of this article. The application development, troubleshooting, and testing described here were performed hands-on.

1. Application Architecture

Before starting the development, let's understand the main components of the application.

Our application consists of the following artifacts:

Artifact Object Name

Database TableZSTD_TABLE_DEMO
Interface CDS ViewZ_I_STD
Projection CDS ViewZ_C_STD
Base Behavior DefinitionZ_I_STD
Behavior PoolZBP_I_STD
Projection Behavior DefinitionZ_C_STD
Metadata ExtensionZ_C_STD
Service DefinitionZ_SD_STD
Service BindingOData V2 - UI

The database table stores the data, CDS Views define the data model and its projection, Behavior Definitions control transactional operations, and the service layer exposes the application to SAP Fiori.

2. Create the Database Table

Object Name: ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO

The first step is creating a database table to store student information.

In Eclipse ADT, create a new Database Table and add the following code:

@EndUserText.label : 'STUDENT TABLE'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #C
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #ALLOWED

define table zstd_table_demo {

  key client       : abap.clnt not null;
  key rollno       : sysuuid_x16 not null;

  studentname      : abap.char(100);
  studentclass     : abap.char(2);
  studentage       : abap.numc(3);
  schoolname       : abap.char(150);

}

Explanation

The table contains student information such as Name, Class, Age, and School Name.

The rollno field uses sysuuid_x16 as the primary key.

This allows us to use automatic UUID generation through the RAP Managed Runtime.

Note: This learning example uses delivery class #C. For a typical transactional application that stores business data, #A is generally more appropriate.

Activate the table using Ctrl + F3.

3. Create the Interface CDS View

Object Name: Z_I_STD

Next, we create the Interface CDS View.

This view represents the underlying data model of our RAP Business Object.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'BASIC VIEW FOR STD'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true

define root view entity Z_I_STD
  as select from zstd_table_demo
{
  key rollno       as Rollno,
      studentname  as Studentname,
      studentclass as Studentclass,
      studentage   as Studentage,
      schoolname   as Schoolname
}

Explanation

The Interface CDS View reads data from the database table and defines the entity structure.

We use define root view entity because this is the root entity of our RAP Business Object.

The Rollno field is defined as the key.

The CDS View can also be used to define associations and compositions in more advanced RAP applications.

Key Learning: The Interface CDS View defines the core data model.

4. Create the Projection CDS View

Object Name: Z_C_STD

The next step is creating a Projection CDS View based on our Interface CDS View.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'CONSUMPTION VIEW FOR STD'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true

define root view entity Z_C_STD
  as projection on Z_I_STD
{
  key Rollno,
      Studentname,
      Studentclass,
      Studentage,
      Schoolname
}

Explanation

The Projection CDS View defines which fields are exposed to service consumers.

In this example, we expose all the fields from our Interface CDS View.

However, in real applications, we can expose only selected fields.

For example, an administrator and a teacher could use different projection views built on the same underlying business object.

Important Difference:

  • Interface CDS View: Defines the underlying data model.

  • Projection CDS View: Defines the projected data available to consumers.

  • Metadata Extension: Controls how the data appears in Fiori.

The annotation @Metadata.allowExtensions: true enables metadata extensions for our projection.

5. Create the Base Behavior Definition

Behavior Definition for: Z_I_STD

Now we define the transactional behavior of our application.

Since we are using Managed RAP, the RAP framework handles standard database persistence operations automatically.

managed implementation in class zbp_i_std unique;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_I_STD alias _studentdetail
persistent table zstd_table_demo
lock master
authorization master ( instance )
{
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;
}

Explanation

Let's understand the important statements.

Managed Implementation

The RAP framework handles the standard Create, Update, and Delete persistence operations.

Persistent Table

The statement persistent table zstd_table_demo defines where our business object data is stored.

Lock Master

Defines the root entity as the lock master.

Authorization Master

Enables instance-level authorization control, which requires a corresponding implementation in the behavior pool.

Managed Numbering

field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;

This enables automatic UUID generation.

We do not need to manually generate the student UUID during creation.

6. Create the Behavior Implementation Class

Object Name: ZBP_I_STD

The Behavior Pool contains custom implementation logic required by the RAP Business Object.

In Managed RAP, we do not need to manually implement standard database CRUD persistence.

However, we declared instance authorization in the Base Behavior Definition, so we must provide the corresponding authorization handler.

Global Behavior Pool Class

CLASS zbp_i_std DEFINITION
  PUBLIC
  ABSTRACT
  FINAL
  FOR BEHAVIOR OF Z_I_STD.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS zbp_i_std IMPLEMENTATION.

ENDCLASS.

Local Handler Class

In the Behavior Pool's Local Types, the instance authorization method can be implemented as follows:

CLASS lhc_Student DEFINITION
  INHERITING FROM cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  PRIVATE SECTION.

    METHODS get_instance_authorizations
      FOR INSTANCE AUTHORIZATION
      IMPORTING keys
      REQUEST requested_authorizations
      FOR _studentdetail
      RESULT result.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS lhc_Student IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD get_instance_authorizations.

    result = VALUE #(
      FOR key IN keys
      (
        %tky    = key-%tky
        %update = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
        %delete = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
      )
    ).

  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.

Explanation

The method get_instance_authorizations determines whether operations are authorized for specific business object instances.

In this simplified learning example, Update and Delete operations are allowed without checking a real authorization object.

Important: This permissive implementation is for demonstration only. A productive application must implement appropriate authorization checks. Use the handler declarations generated by ADT if they differ from this example.

7. Create the Projection Behavior Definition

Behavior Definition for: Z_C_STD

After defining the Base Behavior, we create the Projection Behavior Definition.

projection;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_C_STD alias _studentdetail
{
  use create;
  use update;
  use delete;
}

Explanation

The Base Behavior Definition defines the operations supported by the Business Object.

The Projection Behavior Definition exposes selected operations to consumers.

For example:

  • create; in the Base BDEF defines the Create operation.

  • use create; in the Projection BDEF exposes that operation.

No separate behavior implementation class is required for these projected standard operations.

8. Create the Metadata Extension

Metadata Extension for: Z_C_STD

Now we define how our application should look in SAP Fiori Elements.

Instead of placing UI annotations directly in the CDS View, we use a Metadata Extension.

@Metadata.layer: #CORE

annotate entity Z_C_STD with
{
  @UI.facet: [{
    type: #IDENTIFICATION_REFERENCE,
    position: 1,
    label: 'STUDENT DETAIL'
  }]

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 1, label: 'Student ID' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 1, label: 'Student ID' }]
  Rollno;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 2, label: 'Student name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 2, label: 'Student name' }]
  Studentname;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 3, label: 'Student Class' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 3, label: 'Student Class' }]
  Studentclass;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 4, label: 'Student Age' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 4, label: 'Student Age' }]
  Studentage;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 5, label: 'School name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 5, label: 'School name' }]
  Schoolname;
}

Explanation

The most important UI annotations in this example are:

@UI.lineItem

Defines the fields displayed as columns in the Fiori List Report.

@UI.identification

Defines the fields displayed in the identification section of the Object Page.

@UI.facet

Defines sections within the Object Page.

Using Metadata Extensions helps separate the UI design from the underlying business data model.

9. Create the Service Definition

Object Name: Z_SD_STD

After completing the CDS Views and Behavior Definitions, we create a Service Definition.

@EndUserText.label: 'SERVICE DEFINITION FOR STD'

define service Z_SD_STD {
  expose Z_C_STD;
}

Explanation

The Service Definition identifies which CDS entity will be exposed to external consumers.

Here, we expose the Projection CDS View Z_C_STD.

This keeps the service focused on the consumption model rather than exposing the underlying interface entity directly.

10. Create the Service Binding

Service Binding: Z_UI_STD_O2

The final development step is creating a Service Binding.

In Eclipse ADT:

  1. Right-click the package and create a new Service Binding.

  2. Enter the name Z_UI_STD_O2.

  3. Select the Service Definition Z_SD_STD.

  4. Choose OData V2 - UI as the binding type.

  5. Activate the Service Binding.

  6. Publish the service using the available publishing option.

  7. Select the exposed entity and launch the Fiori Elements Preview.

The availability of OData binding types depends on the backend release.

Explanation

The Service Definition determines what is exposed.

The Service Binding determines how the service is exposed through the selected OData protocol.

In this example, we used OData V2 - UI to generate a SAP Fiori Elements application preview.

11. Testing the Application

After launching the Fiori Elements Preview, the Student Management application displayed the student fields configured in the Metadata Extension.

I created student records and verified that the generated UUIDs were assigned automatically.

The List Report successfully displayed the persisted student data.

The Behavior Definition also exposes Update and Delete operations. These should be tested individually to verify the complete CRUD scenario.

12. Challenges and Troubleshooting

During development, I encountered two interesting issues.

Challenge 1 — Fiori Preview Connectivity

Initially, the Fiori Elements Preview was not accessible because the generated service URL used a hostname and port that were not reachable from my environment.

To investigate the problem, I checked:

  • SMICM — HTTP and HTTPS services.

  • SICF — ICF service activation.

  • HTTPURLLOC — URL generation configuration.

  • Network connectivity to the SAP application server.

After identifying a working HTTPS endpoint, I was able to launch the application preview.

This experience highlighted the importance of SAP system connectivity and proper HTTP/HTTPS configuration.

Challenge 2 — Runtime Error During Create

When I initially tried creating a student, the application returned:

RAISE_SHORTDUMP

I opened transaction ST22 and found the following error:

CX_RAP_HANDLER_NOT_IMPLEMENTED

Handler not implemented
Method: INSTANCE_AUTHORIZATION

The reason was that I had declared:

authorization master ( instance )

But I had not implemented the corresponding authorization handler.

After implementing get_instance_authorizations in the Behavior Pool, the missing-handler error was resolved, and student creation worked successfully.

Key Learning

If we declare authorization handling in a RAP Behavior Definition, we must implement the required authorization methods.

ST22 is a valuable tool for investigating backend runtime errors during RAP development.

13. What I Learned

Building this application helped me understand several important SAP RAP concepts:

  1. How to create persistent tables using ABAP Dictionary DDL.

  2. The purpose of Interface and Projection CDS View Entities.

  3. How Managed RAP handles standard transactional persistence.

  4. How Behavior Definitions define supported operations.

  5. How Behavior Pools implement custom behavior and authorization.

  6. How Metadata Extensions configure SAP Fiori Elements applications.

  7. How Service Definitions and Service Bindings expose OData services.

  8. How to investigate runtime issues using SAP diagnostic tools.

Conclusion

Building my first SAP RAP Student Management Application was a valuable hands-on learning experience.

It helped me understand how the different components of the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model work together to deliver an OData-based transactional application.

Starting from a database table, I built a Managed RAP Business Object, exposed it through an OData V2 service, and successfully displayed and created student records using SAP Fiori Elements.

entry.title: My First SAP RAP Application – Part 2: Advanced RAP Features with Managed RAP
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community! 👋

Welcome to Part 2 of my SAP RAP learning journey!

In my previous blog, "My First SAP RAP Application: Building a Student Management App Using Managed RAP," I explained how I created a simple Student Management Application from scratch using the SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The application supported basic CRUD operations using Managed RAP and SAP Fiori Elements.

https://community.sap.com/t5/abap-blog-posts/my-first-sap-rap-application-building-a-student-management-app-using/ba-p/14506725 

In this second part, I will share how I enhanced the same application by adding more advanced RAP features.

The goal was to move beyond basic CRUD and understand how to implement real business logic and improve the user experience.

What Are We Going to Build?

We will enhance our existing Student Management Application with five features:

  1. Selection Fields — Filter students directly from the Fiori List Report.

  2. Validations — Prevent saving students with invalid ages.

  3. Determinations — Automatically set the initial student status.

  4. Custom Actions — Approve selected students using a custom button.

  5. Draft Handling — Save unfinished changes and continue editing later.

Development Environment

  • SAP S/4HANA 2023 FPS01

  • ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse

  • ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model

  • Managed Business Object

  • SAP Fiori Elements

  • OData V2 UI for the original application

  • OData V4 UI for the draft-enabled application

We will reuse the following objects from Part 1:

Object Name

Database TableZSTD_TABLE_DEMO
Interface CDS ViewZ_I_STD
Projection CDS ViewZ_C_STD
Base Behavior DefinitionZ_I_STD
Behavior PoolZBP_I_STD
Projection Behavior DefinitionZ_C_STD
Service DefinitionZ_SD_STD

Let's get started!

My Personal Experience

After successfully building my first Student Management Application using Managed RAP, I wanted to take the next step and explore more advanced RAP features through hands-on practice.

I started by adding Selection Fields to improve filtering in the Fiori List Report. Then, I implemented a Validation for student age and a Determination to automatically assign the status NEW when creating a student.

One of my favorite parts was implementing the Approve Student action. It was interesting to see how a custom action defined in the RAP Behavior Definition could be implemented in the Behavior Pool and exposed as a button in SAP Fiori Elements.

The most challenging part for me was Draft Handling. I initially faced an error related to draft persistence. After configuring and generating the Draft Table correctly, I was able to create a student, leave the page without activating the record, and find the unfinished record again using the Own Draft filter.

This experience helped me better understand how RAP handles business logic, transactional processing, and draft management.

AI Disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help organize, structure, and improve the English writing of this article. The development, troubleshooting, and testing described in this blog are based on my hands-on SAP RAP learning experience.

1. Adding Selection Fields to the Fiori List Report

The first enhancement was adding filters to the application.

Previously, our List Report displayed student records, but we wanted users to filter the results by Student Name and Student Class.

SAP Fiori Elements allows us to configure these filters using UI annotations.

Step 1: Open the Metadata Extension

Open the Metadata Extension of Z_C_STD.

Add the @UI.selectionField annotation to the relevant fields.

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
@UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }]
Studentname;

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
@UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
Studentclass;

Explanation

The annotation @UI.selectionField tells Fiori Elements to display the specified field in the Filter Bar.

The position property determines the order of the filters.

The important point is that we did not need to write any custom SAPUI5 or JavaScript code.

After activating the Metadata Extension and refreshing the Fiori application, the new filters appeared automatically.

Key Learning

@UI.selectionField Provides field-specific filtering. It is different from the global free-text search feature, which uses @searchannotations.

2. Implementing a Validation for Student Age

Next, I wanted to implement a simple business rule.

Our requirement was:

A student's age must be between 5 and 100.

If the user enters an age outside this range, the application must prevent the final save and display an error message.

Step 1: Define the Validation in the Base Behavior Definition

Open the Base Behavior Definition of Z_I_STD.

Add the following code inside the behavior entity:

validation ValidateStudentAge on save
{
  create;
  field Studentage;
}

Explanation

  • validation defines a business rule.

  • ValidateStudentAge is the name of our validation.

  • on save means the validation runs during the save sequence.

  • create triggers the validation when creating a student.

  • field Studentage triggers it when the age field is changed.

Step 2: Implement the Validation in the Behavior Pool

Open the Behavior Pool ZBP_I_STD.

In the local handler class, declare the method:

METHODS validateStudentAge FOR VALIDATE ON SAVE
  IMPORTING keys FOR _studentdetail~ValidateStudentAge.

Then implement the method:

METHOD validateStudentAge.

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    FIELDS ( Studentage )
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  LOOP AT lt_students INTO DATA(ls_student).

    DATA(lv_age) = CONV i( ls_student-Studentage ).

    IF lv_age < 5 OR lv_age > 100.

      APPEND VALUE #(
        %tky = ls_student-%tky
      ) TO failed-_studentdetail.

      APPEND VALUE #(
        %tky = ls_student-%tky
        %msg = new_message_with_text(
          severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
          text     = 'Student age must be between 5 and 100'
        )
        %element-Studentage = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
      ) TO reported-_studentdetail.

    ENDIF.

  ENDLOOP.

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

The implementation has three main parts.

READ ENTITIES

Reads student data from the RAP transactional buffer, including changes that have not yet been persisted to the database.

FAILED

Identifies the student instances whose save operation must be rejected.

REPORTED

Returns an error message to the consumer and identifies the field containing the invalid value.

Step 3: Test the Validation

Open the Fiori application and try creating a student with:

  • Student Age = 120 → Save should fail.

  • Student Age = 25 → Save should succeed.

Key Learning

RAP Validations allow us to enforce business rules in the backend.

This is important because the validation is not limited to a particular UI.

For more advanced draft scenarios, state messages and message lifecycle handling should also be considered.

3. Using Determinations to Set the Initial Student Status

After implementing the validation, I wanted to automate a small business process.

The requirement was:

Whenever a new student is created, the application should automatically set the student status to NEW.

This is a perfect use case for a RAP Determination.

Step 1: Add a Status Field to the Database Table

Open ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO and add:

student_status : abap.char(10);

This field stores the student status.

We will use two values:

  • NEW

  • APPROVED

Step 2: Extend the Interface CDS View

In Z_I_STD, add:

student_status as StudentStatus

Step 3: Extend the Projection CDS View

In Z_C_STD, expose the new field:

StudentStatus

Step 4: Display the Status in Fiori

In the Metadata Extension, add:

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
StudentStatus;

Step 5: Define the Determination

In the Base Behavior Definition, add:

field ( readonly ) StudentStatus;

determination SetInitialStatus on modify
{
  create;
}

Explanation

on modify tells RAP to execute the determination during the modify phase when its trigger condition is met.

The create trigger means it runs when a new student instance is created.

We marked StudentStatus as read-only so the consumer cannot freely change it. Our backend logic will manage its value.

Step 6: Implement the Determination

In the Behavior Pool, declare:

METHODS SetInitialStatus FOR DETERMINE ON MODIFY
  IMPORTING keys FOR _studentdetail~SetInitialStatus.

Implementation:

METHOD SetInitialStatus.

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  DELETE lt_students WHERE StudentStatus IS NOT INITIAL.

  CHECK lt_students IS NOT INITIAL.

  MODIFY ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    UPDATE FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH VALUE #(
      FOR ls_student IN lt_students
      (
        %tky          = ls_student-%tky
        StudentStatus = 'NEW'
      )
    ).

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

First, we read the Student Status.

If the status is already filled, we do not overwrite it.

If the status is empty, we update it to NEW using MODIFY ENTITIES IN LOCAL MODE.

Since this is Managed RAP, the framework handles persistence when the active instance is saved.

Step 7: Test the Determination

Create a student in Fiori.

The Student Status should be set automatically to NEW.

Key Learning

A Validation checks whether data is valid.

A Determination automatically calculates or changes data when defined trigger conditions are met.

4. Creating a Custom Action: Approve Student

Now that every new student receives the status NEW, I wanted to add a button that allows the user to approve a selected student.

The business requirement was:

Select a student in the List Report, click Approve Student, and change the status from NEW to APPROVED.

In RAP, we can achieve this using a Custom Instance Action.

Step 1: Define the Action in the Base Behavior Definition

Open the Base BDEF Z_I_STD and add:

action ( authorization : update ) ApproveStudent
  result [1] $self;

Explanation

  • action defines a custom business operation.

  • ApproveStudent is the action name.

  • authorization : update reuses update authorization for this action.

  • result [1] $self returns the updated student instance.

Step 2: Expose the Action in the Projection Behavior Definition

Open the Projection BDEF Z_C_STD and add:

use action ApproveStudent;

The Base Behavior Definition defines the action, while the Projection Behavior Definition makes it available to the service consumer.

Step 3: Implement the Action in the Behavior Pool

Declare the method:

METHODS ApproveStudent FOR MODIFY
  IMPORTING keys FOR ACTION _studentdetail~ApproveStudent
  RESULT result.

Implementation:

METHOD ApproveStudent.

  MODIFY ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    UPDATE FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH VALUE #(
      FOR key IN keys
      (
        %tky          = key-%tky
        StudentStatus = 'APPROVED'
      )
    ).

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    ALL FIELDS
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  result = VALUE #(
    FOR ls_student IN lt_students
    (
      %tky   = ls_student-%tky
      %param = ls_student
    )
  ).

ENDMETHOD.

Explanation

The method receives the keys of the selected students.

Using MODIFY ENTITIES, it changes their status to APPROVED.

Then it reads the updated instances and returns them to the consumer.

Step 4: Add the Action Button to the Fiori List Report

To display the action in the application, update the StudentStatus annotations in the Metadata Extension.

@UI.lineItem: [
  { position: 60, label: 'Student Status' },
  {
    type: #FOR_ACTION,
    dataAction: 'ApproveStudent',
    label: 'Approve Student'
  }
]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
StudentStatus;

The #FOR_ACTION annotation allows Fiori Elements to generate the action button automatically.

Step 5: Test the Action

Open the List Report, select a student whose status is NEW, and click Approve Student.

The status should change to APPROVED.

Key Learning

RAP Actions allow us to implement custom business operations beyond standard CRUD.

In a future enhancement, Dynamic Feature Control could be used to disable the Approve action for students who are already approved.

5. Enabling Draft Handling

The final enhancement was Draft Handling.

This feature was particularly interesting because it allows users to work on unfinished data without immediately activating it as a final database record.

For example, a user might start entering student information, leave the application, and return later to continue editing.

What Is Draft Handling?

Draft Handling separates unfinished changes from active business data.

A draft-enabled RAP Business Object supports operations such as:

  • Edit

  • Resume

  • Activate

  • Discard

  • Prepare

The RAP framework manages the draft lifecycle.

Step 1: Add Timestamp Fields to the Database Table

Open ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO and add:

last_changed_at       : abp_lastchange_tstmpl;
local_last_changed_at : abp_locinst_lastchange_tstmpl;

These fields are used to track changes and support ETag-based concurrency control.

Step 2: Extend the Interface CDS View

Add the following fields to Z_I_STD:

@Semantics.systemDateTime.lastChangedAt: true
last_changed_at as LastChangedAt,

@Semantics.systemDateTime.localInstanceLastChangedAt: true
local_last_changed_at as LocalLastChangedAt

The semantic annotations allow the managed runtime to maintain the corresponding administrative timestamps.

Step 3: Extend the Projection CDS View

Expose the following field in Z_C_STD:

LocalLastChangedAt

LastChangedAt is used as the total ETag for draft processing and does not need to be exposed through this projection.

Step 4: Enable Draft in the Base Behavior Definition

Add with draft; and configure the draft persistence and ETags.

The following example shows the final Base Behavior Definition after including the enhancements from this blog:

managed implementation in class zbp_i_std unique;
strict ( 2 );

with draft;

define behavior for Z_I_STD alias _studentdetail
persistent table zstd_table_demo
draft table zstd_table_d
lock master
total etag LastChangedAt
authorization master ( instance )
etag master LocalLastChangedAt
{
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;
  field ( readonly ) StudentStatus;
  field ( readonly ) LastChangedAt, LocalLastChangedAt;

  validation ValidateStudentAge on save
  {
    create;
    field Studentage;
  }

  determination SetInitialStatus on modify
  {
    create;
  }

  action ( authorization : update ) ApproveStudent
    result [1] $self;

  draft action Edit;
  draft action Activate;
  draft action Discard;
  draft action Resume;

  draft determine action Prepare
  {
    validation ValidateStudentAge;
  }

  mapping for zstd_table_demo
  {
    Rollno             = rollno;

Key Takeaways

This project helped me understand the difference between several important RAP concepts.

Validation vs. Determination

A Validation checks the consistency of data and can reject invalid changes.

A Determination automatically performs business logic when its trigger conditions are met.

Action vs. Standard CRUD

Create, Update, and Delete are standard operations, while Actions allow us to implement custom business processes such as Approve Student.

Draft vs. Active Data

Draft instances hold unfinished changes, while active instances represent the final persisted business data.

RAP Backend vs. Fiori Elements

RAP handles the transactional business logic, while Fiori Elements can generate much of the application interface based on metadata and exposed behavior.

This significantly reduces the amount of custom frontend code needed for standard business applications.
